cases.title: Navkar Logistics Ltd. v. Zenith Shipping Corp.
cases.facts:
On February 1, 2025, Navkar Logistics entered into a high-value, fixed-
price charter party agreement with Zenith Shipping Corp. Zenith agreed to
transport 50,000 metric tons of perishable agricultural goods from Mumbai
to a major port in the Middle East, with a strict delivery deadline of
March 15, 2025. The contract contained a standard Force Majeure clause.
On February 20, while the vessel was en route, a sudden, unpredicted
geopolitical conflict erupted, resulting in a naval blockade of the
primary shipping strait. To reach the destination, Zenith Shipping would
have to reroute the vessel around the horn of Africa, increasing the
voyage time by four weeks and escalating fuel costs by 400%. Zenith
notified Navkar that they were invoking the Force Majeure clause and
terminating the contract due to commercial impossibility, leaving the
perishable cargo stranded at a safe intermediate port. Navkar sued for
breach of contract and specific performance.
cases.issues:
Does a sudden, astronomical increase in operational costs due to a
geopolitical event constitute a Force Majeure event or "impossibility"
under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872?

Does the doctrine of frustration apply when performance remains
physically possible but becomes commercially ruinous for one party?

Is Navkar Logistics entitled to damages for the loss of perishable goods
resulting from the mid-voyage termination?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Navkar Logistics)
Navkar argued that the contract was absolute. Relying on the landmark
English case Tsakiroglou & Co. Ltd. v. Noblee Thorl GmbH (the Suez Canal
closure case) and Indian precedents like Energy Watchdog v. CERC, they
argued that mere commercial hardship, unprofitability, or the necessity
of taking a longer route does not frustrate a contract. Performance was
not physically or legally impossible; it simply became expensive for
Zenith. Navkar argued that shipping companies inherently assume the risk
of route alterations, and invoking Force Majeure was a bad-faith attempt
by Zenith to escape a bad bargain, making them liable for the total loss
of the perishable cargo.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Zenith Shipping)
Zenith argued that the blockade fundamentally altered the foundational
basis of the contract. They asserted that a 400% increase in fuel costs
and a four-week delay transformed the obligation into something radically
different from what was originally undertaken. They relied on Section 56
of the Contract Act, arguing that "impossibility" includes practical
commercial impossibility where performance would result in absolute
financial ruin. Furthermore, they argued that since the cargo was highly
perishable, a four-week delay would render the goods useless anyway,
meaning the central purpose of the contract (delivering fresh goods) was
already frustrated by the blockade.
cases.judgment:
The Commercial Court ruled in favor of Navkar Logistics. Zenith Shipping
was found liable for breach of contract and ordered to pay substantial
compensatory damages. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly interpreted the Doctrine of Frustration under Section
56. The judge affirmed that Indian contract law sets an incredibly high
threshold for frustration. A contract is not frustrated merely because it
becomes onerous or commercially unviable. The Court noted that an
alternative route existed, and Zenith had the physical capacity to
complete the voyage. The risk of fluctuating fuel prices and route
disruptions are standard commercial risks in international shipping.
Because the Force Majeure clause did not explicitly list "blockades" or
"economic hardship" as triggering events, Zenith could not rely on it.
The Court held that Zenith was obligated to complete the voyage and
negotiate the damages for the perished cargo later, rather than
abandoning the goods mid-transit.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case robustly reinforces the Strict Interpretation of the Doctrine
of Frustration (Section 56, Indian Contract Act). It establishes the
vital commercial principle that economic hardship, unprofitability, or
the necessity of a longer, more expensive route does not constitute legal
impossibility or frustration. Parties must explicitly allocate such risks
in their Force Majeure clauses.

cases.title: Prakriti Naturals v. DermaGlow Inc.
cases.facts:
Prakriti Naturals is a highly successful Indian organic skincare brand.
In May 2025, DermaGlow Inc., a massive multinational competitor, launched
a covert marketing campaign. DermaGlow funded a network of prominent
anonymous beauty influencers to publish a coordinated series of viral
videos. These videos falsely claimed that laboratory tests proved
Prakriti's flagship "100% Organic" face cream contained high levels of
carcinogenic synthetic parabens. The videos caused public panic,
resulting in a 60% drop in Prakriti's sales and several retail chains
delisting their products. Upon investigation by cyber authorities, the
funding was traced back to DermaGlow's PR agency. Prakriti Naturals sued
DermaGlow for Trade Libel, Corporate Defamation, and massive exemplary
damages.
cases.issues:
Can a corporate entity be held liable for defamation/trade libel
perpetrated through anonymous third-party influencers?

What are the essential ingredients to prove the tort of "Injurious
Falsehood" or "Trade Libel" against a competitor?

Is Prakriti Naturals entitled to exemplary (punitive) damages for
calculated corporate sabotage?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Prakriti Naturals)
Prakriti Naturals argued that DermaGlow orchestrated a malicious,
premeditated campaign of injurious falsehood. They proved through
independent lab results that their products were 100% organic, rendering
the influencer claims demonstrably false. To establish Trade Libel, the
plaintiff must prove the statements were false, published maliciously,
and caused special damage. Prakriti provided financial audits proving a
direct 60% revenue drop corresponding exactly with the viral campaign.
They demanded exemplary damages, arguing that standard compensatory
damages would merely be treated as a "cost of doing business" by the
multinational giant.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (DermaGlow Inc.)
DermaGlow attempted to distance itself from the influencers, claiming the
PR agency acted as an independent contractor and exceeded its brief. They
argued they could not be held vicariously liable for the independent
opinions expressed by influencers on social media platforms. Furthermore,
they argued that corporate entities cannot sue for defamation in the same
manner as living persons, as they have no "feelings" to be hurt, and must
strictly prove quantifiable, direct financial loss attributable solely to
the statements, not general market fluctuation.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled decisively in favor of Prakriti Naturals. DermaGlow
was held vicariously liable for Trade Libel and ordered to pay both
compensatory and massive exemplary damages. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on modern corporate sabotage. The
judge pierced the veil of the PR agency, ruling that DermaGlow was the
principal architect of the campaign and is absolutely vicariously liable
for torts committed by its agents in the course of aggressive marketing.
The Court outlined the elements of Trade Libel: malicious publication of
false statements concerning a plaintiff's goods, leading to special
damage. The coordinated nature of the attack proved malice. The 60% drop
in sales proved special damage. The Court heavily penalized DermaGlow,
ruling that deploying anonymous influencers to spread lethal, calculated
lies about a competitor's product safety is a grotesque abuse of market
power, justifying exemplary damages to serve as a severe deterrent
against corporate "black PR."
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case modernizes the tort of Injurious Falsehood / Trade Libel for
the social media age. It establishes the principle of Vicarious Liability
for Astroturfing/Influencer Campaigns, and affirms the courts'
willingness to award Exemplary Damages against corporations that utilize
calculated, malicious falsehoods to destroy a competitor's market share.

cases.title: Rao v. State Highways Authority
cases.facts:
Mr. Rao owned a large, landlocked agricultural estate. For 40 years, his
only access to the main public road was a 15-foot wide dirt path running
through the property of his neighbor, Mr. Singh. This access was a
legally recognized "Easement of Necessity." In 2024, the State Highways
Authority invoked eminent domain to construct a massive elevated
expressway. The expressway completely bisected Mr. Singh's property,
obliterating the dirt path. However, the Authority constructed a new,
paved service road on the opposite side of Mr. Rao's estate, giving him
direct, superior access to the highway. Despite this new access, Mr. Rao
sued Mr. Singh and the Authority, demanding they build an underpass to
restore his historical dirt path, claiming his easement rights were
absolute and perpetual.
cases.issues:
Does an "Easement of Necessity" under the Indian Easements Act, 1882,
extinguish automatically when the necessity ceases to exist?

Can the State's acquisition of the servient heritage (Singh's land)
extinguish a private easement right held by the dominant heritage (Rao)?

Is the dominant owner entitled to compensation for the loss of an
easement if alternative, superior access is provided?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. Rao)
Mr. Rao argued that his right of way had matured into an absolute
property right through 40 years of continuous use (Easement by
Prescription), not just necessity. He argued that the State cannot
extinguish a vested property right without specific compensation. He
contended that the new service road was on the opposite side of his
estate, requiring him to re-route his internal farm operations, causing
significant inconvenience. He demanded the restoration of his historical
pathway via an underpass, arguing that easements run with the land in
perpetuity.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State Highways & Mr. Singh)
The Defendants relied strictly on Section 41 of the Indian Easements Act,
which states that an easement of necessity is extinguished when the
necessity comes to an end. They argued that because the State provided
Mr. Rao with a brand-new, paved public service road directly connecting
his property to the highway, his land was no longer landlocked. The
"necessity" for traversing Mr. Singh's land had completely vanished.
Furthermore, they argued that eminent domain extinguishes all prior
private encumbrances on the acquired land, and since Rao suffered no
actual loss of access, no compensation was due.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court dismissed Mr. Rao's suit. The Court ruled that the
easement was extinguished by law, and no underpass or compensation was
required. The Defendants prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court applied a strict, literal interpretation of the Indian
Easements Act. The judge clarified that an Easement of Necessity is not
an absolute, permanent transfer of land ownership; it is a conditional
right born of absolute need. The law does not favor burdening one man's
property for another's convenience if an alternative exists. The Court
ruled that the moment the State provided the new service road, Mr. Rao's
estate ceased to be landlocked. Consequently, under Section 41, the
easement of necessity was instantly and automatically extinguished. The
Court also dismissed the "prescription" argument, noting that a right
born of necessity cannot simultaneously be claimed as an adverse
prescriptive right. Mere internal inconvenience for Mr. Rao does not
justify burdening the State with the cost of an underpass or restricting
the servient owner's property.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case firmly enforces Section 41 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882.
It establishes the fundamental property law principle that an Easement of
Necessity is strictly coterminous with the necessity itself. The moment
an alternative, lawful access to a public way is established, the
easement is automatically extinguished, prioritizing the unencumbered
ownership of the servient heritage.

cases.title: Sharma v. Kapoor Surrogacy Clinic
cases.facts:
Mr. and Mrs. Sharma, an infertile couple, entered into an altruistic
surrogacy agreement with a close relative, Geeta, facilitated by the
Kapoor Surrogacy Clinic, strictly in compliance with the Surrogacy
(Regulation) Act, 2021. Geeta was implanted with an embryo created from
Mr. Sharma's sperm and a donor egg. During the seventh month of the
pregnancy, Mr. and Mrs. Sharma tragically died in a commercial airline
crash. They left behind no will. Upon the birth of the child, Geeta (the
surrogate) refused to hand the child over to the state orphanage,
claiming she had formed a deep maternal bond and wished to adopt the
child. However, Mr. Sharma's brother, Anil, filed a petition claiming
legal custody and guardianship of the child as the closest blood relative
and legal heir to the Sharma estate.
cases.issues:
In the event of the untimely death of the intending parents before the
birth of the child, who holds the paramount right to legal custody and
guardianship under the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021?

Does a gestational surrogate mother, who has no genetic link to the child
but carried it to term, possess any legal standing to claim custody or
adoption rights?

How does the Court determine the "welfare of the child" in complex
assisted reproductive technology (ART) scenarios?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Anil Sharma - Uncle)
Anil Sharma argued that under the Surrogacy Act, the intending parents
are the absolute legal parents of the child from the moment of
conception. Upon their death, the child becomes an orphan, but retains
its status as a legitimate heir to the Sharma family. Anil argued that as
the closest living genetic and legal relative (paternal uncle), he is the
natural guardian under the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act. He argued
that Geeta, acting merely as a gestational carrier under a statutory
contract, has absolutely no legal or genetic rights to the child and
cannot bypass formal adoption procedures by exploiting a tragedy to claim
custody.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Geeta - Surrogate)
Geeta argued on the grounds of equity and the paramount welfare of the
child. She contended that while the statute dictates the intending
parents are the legal parents, the law is silent on custody disputes
arising from their sudden death prior to birth. She argued that having
nourished and carried the child for nine months, she was the only living
person with a profound biological and psychological bond to the infant.
She argued that tearing the newborn away from the only maternal presence
it knows to hand it over to an uncle (who only seeks custody to control
the deceased brother's massive estate) fundamentally violates the best
interests of the child.
cases.judgment:
The Family Court ruled in favor of Anil Sharma regarding legal
guardianship, but established a unique framework prioritizing the child's
welfare. Geeta's claim for absolute custody was dismissed. The Plaintiff
prevailed in law.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly applied the provisions of the Surrogacy (Regulation)
Act, 2021. The judge emphasized that the legislative intent of the Act is
to completely sever the legal and parental rights of the surrogate mother
to prevent custody battles and commercial exploitation. The law
explicitly states the child is the biological child of the intending
parents. Therefore, Geeta possessed zero legal standing to claim
maternity or automatic custody.

However, exercising its parens patriae jurisdiction (the state as the
ultimate guardian of children), the Court prioritized the "welfare of the
child." The judge recognized Anil as the legal guardian and heir to the
estate. Yet, recognizing Geeta's altruistic sacrifice and the infant's
immediate psychological needs, the Court ordered a transitional
guardianship. Anil was granted legal custody, but the Court mandated
heavily supervised visitation rights for Geeta for the first two years,
and ordered the state child welfare committee to rigorously monitor Anil
to ensure he was providing genuine care and not merely securing the child
to control the Sharma inheritance.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a vital precedent interpreting the Surrogacy (Regulation)
Act, 2021. It legally cements the principle that a gestational surrogate
has absolutely no legal, maternal, or custody rights over the child, even
in the event of the intending parents' death. However, it affirms that
the Courts retain inherent parens patriae jurisdiction to impose
conditions on the legal guardians to ensure the absolute welfare of the
child.

cases.title: GreenEarth NGO v. ChemCorp Industries
cases.facts:
ChemCorp Industries, a multi-billion dollar publicly traded chemical
conglomerate, established a wholly-owned subsidiary, "EcoSolv Pvt. Ltd.,"
to manage the disposal of highly toxic industrial effluents generated by
ChemCorp's main factories. EcoSolv was severely undercapitalized,
possessed no independent board of directors (the board comprised junior
ChemCorp employees), and operated entirely on ChemCorp's premises. Over
five years, EcoSolv systematically and illegally dumped thousands of tons
of carcinogenic waste into a local river, causing a massive ecological
disaster and a spike in local cancer rates.

GreenEarth NGO filed a massive civil class-action tort suit. Recognizing
that the subsidiary (EcoSolv) was intentionally kept bankrupt to avoid
paying damages, the NGO sued the parent company, ChemCorp Industries,
directly for ₹500 Crores. ChemCorp moved to dismiss the suit, invoking
the absolute principle of separate legal entity and limited liability,
arguing they were merely a shareholder in EcoSolv and not legally
responsible for its operational torts.
cases.issues:
Under what specific circumstances can a civil court "pierce the corporate
veil" to hold a parent company liable for the environmental torts
committed by a wholly-owned subsidiary?

Does the creation of an undercapitalized subsidiary specifically designed
to absorb hazardous operational risks constitute a "sham" or "facade"
under corporate law?

Can the principles of Absolute Liability be extended upwards through
corporate structures to reach the "deep pockets" of the parent entity?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (GreenEarth NGO)
The NGO argued that EcoSolv was a mere corporate shell-a deliberate,
malicious facade erected by ChemCorp to execute environmental crimes
while shielding its massive profits from liability. Relying on the
landmark M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Absolute Liability) and
international jurisprudence like Chandler v. Cape plc, the NGO argued
that the parent company exercised absolute, day-to-day control over the
subsidiary. EcoSolv had no independent mind, capital, or operations. The
NGO urged the court to pierce the corporate veil in the interest of
public policy and environmental justice, asserting that multinational
polluters cannot use legal fictions to externalize the catastrophic costs
of their hazardous activities onto the public.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (ChemCorp Industries)
ChemCorp hid firmly behind the bedrock of corporate law: Salomon v. A
Salomon & Co Ltd. They argued that a parent company and its subsidiary
are distinct, separate legal persons. Limited liability is the engine of
modern capitalism. They argued that creating subsidiaries to manage
specific high-risk operations is a standard, lawful corporate
restructuring practice, not a fraud. ChemCorp argued that to pierce the
veil, the plaintiff must prove that the subsidiary was created
specifically to evade an existing, pre-determined legal obligation, which
was not the case here, as the pollution occurred after incorporation.
cases.judgment:
The National Green Tribunal (NGT) and subsequently the Supreme Court
ruled in favor of GreenEarth NGO. The corporate veil was pierced, and
ChemCorp Industries was held absolutely and directly liable to pay the
₹500 Crores in environmental restoration and victim compensation. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a devastating blow to corporate evasion tactics. The
judge acknowledged the Salomon principle but unequivocally stated it is
not an impenetrable shield for toxic torts. The Court adopted the "Alter
Ego" and "Single Economic Entity" tests. The judge examined the
operational reality: EcoSolv shared premises, directors, and financial
lifelines with ChemCorp. It was grossly undercapitalized, proving it was
never intended to operate independently or possess the capacity to pay
for the massive risks it handled.

The Court ruled that when a parent company creates a "sham" subsidiary
expressly to handle inherently dangerous and hazardous activities, and
maintains absolute operational control, the parent company assumes a
direct duty of care to the public. Applying the doctrine of Absolute
Liability, the Court held that the enterprise taking the profit from the
hazardous activity must bear the absolute burden of its devastation.
Allowing ChemCorp to escape liability by hiding behind a bankrupt paper
company would make a mockery of environmental justice and the "Polluter
Pays" principle.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes a monumental precedent for Piercing the Corporate
Veil in Environmental Torts. It creates the legal principle that parent
companies cannot use undercapitalized, fully-controlled "sham"
subsidiaries as liability shields for hazardous activities. Courts will
apply the Single Economic Entity doctrine and Absolute Liability to hold
the deep-pocketed parent directly accountable for mass environmental
damage.

cases.title: Café Royal v. Royal Brews Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
"Café Royal" is an ultra-luxury, heritage coffeehouse established in
Mumbai in 1910. It is renowned globally, frequented by royalty and
celebrities, and holds a registered trademark for "Café Royal" in Class
43 (providing food and drink). The brand is synonymous with extreme
exclusivity and high society. In 2024, a mass-market, low-budget roadside
tea stall franchise registered a company named "Royal Brews Pvt. Ltd."
and began opening hundreds of tin-roofed stalls across India, selling ₹10
cups of tea. Their logo featured a crown highly similar to Café Royal's,
and their signboards prominently displayed "A Royal Brew."

Café Royal filed a suit for Trademark Infringement, Passing Off, and
Trademark Dilution. Royal Brews defended themselves, stating they were in
a completely different market segment (low-income street tea vs. ultra-
luxury dining), meaning there was absolutely no chance of "consumer
confusion"-no one would mistake a ₹10 tea stall for a five-star heritage
café.
cases.issues:
Can a trademark infringement or "passing off" claim succeed when the
competing businesses operate in drastically different price brackets and
market segments, eliminating direct consumer confusion?

Does the use of a similar mark by a low-quality brand constitute
"Trademark Dilution" by blurring or tarnishment under Section 29(4) of
the Trade Marks Act, 1999?

Does the word "Royal" constitute a generic/descriptive term, or has it
acquired secondary meaning and "well-known trademark" status for the
plaintiff?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Café Royal)
Café Royal conceded that direct consumer confusion was unlikely. Instead,
they anchored their case heavily on Section 29(4) of the Trade Marks Act:
Trademark Dilution. They argued that "Café Royal" is a "Well-Known
Trademark" with massive trans-border reputation. They asserted that Royal
Brews was guilty of Dilution by Tarnishment. By associating the
prestigious, luxury "Royal" crest and branding with unhygienic, low-
budget street stalls, the defendant was actively degrading, cheapening,
and destroying the exclusive luxury aura and immense goodwill the
plaintiff had spent a century building. They argued that Royal Brews was
taking a "free ride" on their famous branding.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Royal Brews)
Royal Brews argued that trademark law is designed to prevent consumer
deception, not to grant monopolies over common English words. They argued
"Royal" is a highly descriptive, generic laudatory term used by thousands
of businesses worldwide; therefore, Café Royal cannot claim exclusive
ownership over it. Furthermore, they argued that since the services
(street tea vs. fine dining) and target demographics were worlds apart,
there was zero competitive harm. They asserted that Section 29(4)
requires the mark to have a reputation specifically in India, and merely
using the word "Royal" for a tea stall does not tarnish a luxury cafe.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Café Royal. The Court granted a
permanent injunction restraining Royal Brews from using the word "Royal"
in conjunction with a crown logo, ordering them to rebrand. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a textbook analysis of Trademark Dilution. The judge
first recognized Café Royal as a "Well-Known Trademark" under the Act,
noting its century-long history, media presence, and immense goodwill.
The Court dismissed the defendant's argument regarding "consumer
confusion." Under the doctrine of Dilution (Section 29(4)), protection
extends to dissimilar goods/services if the unauthorized use takes unfair
advantage of, or is detrimental to, the distinctive character or repute
of a famous mark.

The Court heavily emphasized the concept of Tarnishment. The judge ruled
that a luxury brand's primary asset is its aura of exclusivity. Allowing
a mass-market, unhygienic roadside stall to utilize highly similar
branding degrades the prestigious identity of the famous mark in the
public consciousness. While "Royal" is a common word, the specific
combination of the word with a crown logo in the beverage sector clearly
demonstrated a malafide intent by the defendant to piggyback on the
plaintiff's established fame. The Court concluded that protecting the
reputational integrity of a well-known mark supersedes the lack of direct
commercial competition.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case significantly reinforces the doctrine of Trademark Dilution
(Section 29(4) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999). It establishes the legal
principle that a "Well-Known Trademark" can enjoin the use of a similar
mark by a non-competitor in a completely different market segment if such
use causes Dilution by Tarnishment (degrading the luxury or prestigious
reputation of the famous mark).

cases.title: Mehta v. FinAI Securities
cases.facts:
Mr. Mehta, a retired pensioner, invested his entire life savings of ₹50
Lakhs into FinAI Securities, a cutting-edge "Robo-Advisory" and
algorithmic trading platform. FinAI marketed itself as providing "risk-
free, AI-driven portfolio management ensuring guaranteed 12% annual
returns" with a mandatory "stop-loss" feature that would automatically
halt trading if the portfolio dropped by 5%.

On August 12, 2024, a sudden, unprecedented "flash crash" hit the
national stock exchange. FinAI's algorithm malfunctioned
catastrophically. The "stop-loss" code failed to execute due to a server
latency issue. Instead of halting, the AI continuously panic-sold Mehta's
assets at rock-bottom prices. Within ten minutes, Mehta's portfolio was
wiped out, leaving him with ₹2 Lakhs. Mehta filed a complaint with the
National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC), alleging gross
deficiency in service and seeking a full refund of ₹50 Lakhs. FinAI
argued that stock market investments are subject to market risks, and
algorithmic glitches during black-swan events are protected under their
"Limitation of Liability" and Force Majeure clauses.
cases.issues:
Is a retail investor utilizing an automated algorithmic trading platform
considered a "Consumer" under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?

Does a catastrophic software failure in a heavily marketed "risk-
mitigation" feature (stop-loss) constitute a actionable "Deficiency in
Service"?

Can a financial tech company use boilerplate "market risk" and
"limitation of liability" clauses to escape liability for the failure of
their proprietary AI algorithms?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. Mehta)
Mehta argued that he did not pay FinAI to simply access the stock market;
he paid a premium subscription fee specifically for their touted "AI
risk-management service." Relying on the Consumer Protection Act, he
asserted that FinAI provided a defective service. The failure of the
"stop-loss" algorithm-the exact feature he paid for to protect his life
savings-was a fundamental technological deficiency, not a natural market
fluctuation. He argued that FinAI's marketing ("guaranteed returns,"
"risk-free") constituted an Unfair Trade Practice. He demanded that the
NCDRC strike down the "limitation of liability" clause as an
unconscionable, one-sided contract under Section 47 of the Act.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (FinAI Securities)
FinAI argued that financial trading platforms merely act as
intermediaries. The stock market is inherently volatile, and every user
signs a mandatory SEBI-approved disclosure stating that "investments are
subject to market risks." They argued that a "flash crash" is an
unforeseeable market anomaly (Force Majeure), and no algorithmic code can
guarantee 100% execution during extreme server loads. FinAI contended
that holding software companies strictly liable for trading losses would
destroy the fintech sector. They relied heavily on their Terms of
Service, which capped their maximum liability to the subscription fee
paid by the user (₹10,000).
cases.judgment:
The NCDRC ruled overwhelmingly in favor of Mr. Mehta. FinAI Securities
was ordered to refund the lost ₹48 Lakhs to Mehta, along with punitive
damages for unfair trade practices. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Commission delivered a landmark judgment adapting consumer protection
to the fintech era. The NCDRC affirmed that retail investors paying for
advisory and automated trading software are unequivocally "Consumers."
The Commission drew a sharp distinction between a "market loss" (a stock
naturally losing value) and a "service loss" (a loss caused because the
platform's proprietary safety features failed to activate).

The judge ruled that FinAI marketed their algorithm as a shield against
risk. The failure of the stop-loss feature was a pure
software/infrastructure failure-a glaring deficiency in the service they
promised to provide. The Commission aggressively struck down the
Limitation of Liability clause, ruling that a company cannot charge for
an AI risk-management service and then contractually absolve itself when
that exact AI wipes out a consumer's life savings due to poor coding.
Such boilerplate clauses in click-wrap agreements are unconscionable and
void against public policy. Furthermore, promising "guaranteed returns"
in equity markets is illegal and constitutes a deceptive, Unfair Trade
Practice.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a massive precedent for FinTech Accountability under the
Consumer Protection Act, 2019. It establishes that algorithmic failures
(like failed stop-losses) constitute actionable "Deficiencies in
Service", not mere market risks. Furthermore, it affirms that one-sided
"Limitation of Liability" clauses in digital platforms are unconscionable
and void if they seek to insulate the company from the catastrophic
failure of their core proprietary technology.

cases.title: Apex Builders Ltd. v. Metro Rail Corp.
cases.facts:
Apex Builders Ltd. owned a highly valuable, vacant plot of land in the
city center. In 2022, they secured all municipal sanctions to construct a
massive luxury shopping mall. In 2024, the State Metro Rail Corporation
(a public utility) finalized the alignment for a new, crucial underground
metro line. The engineered route required boring a tunnel directly
beneath Apex's plot. While the tunnel was 30 meters underground and would
not technically require demolishing the surface mall, Apex Builders filed
a civil suit seeking a Permanent Prohibitory Injunction to stop the
tunneling.

Apex argued that the deep-earth tunneling would inevitably weaken the
foundation of their planned mega-mall, restricting their right to build
deep basements, and effectively constituting an uncompensated trespass
into their subsurface property rights. The Metro Rail Corp. argued that
stopping the tunnel would derail a multi-billion dollar public transit
project designed to serve millions, and that Apex should only be entitled
to monetary compensation for any actual damages, not an injunction.
cases.issues:
Who owns the subsurface rights of a private property, and does deep
underground tunneling by a public utility constitute an actionable
trespass justifying an injunction?

Under Section 41 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, should a court grant
an injunction against an infrastructural project of immense public
utility?

Must private property rights strictly yield to overriding public interest
in the context of urban infrastructure development?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Builders)
Apex Builders relied on the ancient property maxim Cuius est solum, eius
est usque ad coelum et ad inferos (Whoever owns the soil, it is theirs up
to heaven and down to hell). They argued that their ownership of the land
extends infinitely downward. Unauthorized tunneling by the Metro Corp is
a continuous, blatant trespass. They argued that monetary damages are
inadequate because the presence of the tunnel permanently sterilizes
their ability to construct deep, multi-level underground parking,
severely degrading the commercial viability of their mall. They demanded
an absolute injunction to protect their constitutional right to enjoy
their property without state interference.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Metro Rail Corp.)
Metro Rail Corp. argued that the absolute "heaven to hell" maxim is
obsolete in modern urban jurisprudence. They cited Section 20A of the
Specific Relief Act (introduced in 2018), which strictly prohibits courts
from granting injunctions in infrastructure projects if such an
injunction would cause delay in the progress or completion of the
project. The Metro argued that re-routing the tunnel was technically
impossible and would cost the exchequer thousands of crores. They
asserted that individual property rights must be subordinated to the
greater public good (mass transit for millions), and Apex's remedy lies
exclusively in claiming monetary damages for any proven structural
restrictions, not in halting a sovereign infrastructure project.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court refused to grant the Permanent Injunction to Apex
Builders. The Court allowed the Metro Rail Corp to proceed with the
tunneling, while granting Apex Builders the liberty to file a separate
suit for monetary compensation for the diminution of their land value.
The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court's reasoning was anchored squarely in the 2018 amendments to the
Specific Relief Act and the doctrine of overriding public interest. The
judge acknowledged the plaintiff's subsurface property rights but noted
that equitable remedies like injunctions are discretionary. The Court
heavily relied on Section 20A, ruling that the legislature explicitly
stripped civil courts of the power to halt critical infrastructure
projects via injunctions.

The judge reasoned that granting an injunction would hold a multi-billion
dollar public transit system serving millions of citizens hostage to the
commercial parking needs of a single luxury mall developer. Equity
demands the balancing of convenience. The harm caused to the public by
delaying the metro infinitely outweighs the harm caused to the developer.
The Court ruled that while the tunneling is technically an encumbrance,
it is an unavoidable necessity for urban survival. Apex Builders cannot
stop the project; their sole legal remedy is to quantify the loss of
their basement development potential and sue the State for monetary
compensation.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case rigidly enforces Section 20A of the Specific Relief Act, 1963
(Special provisions for infrastructure projects). It establishes the
absolute legal principle that courts cannot grant prohibitory injunctions
against critical public infrastructure projects. Private property rights
must yield to overriding public utility, restricting the landowner's
remedy exclusively to claims for monetary compensation for damages or
loss of land value.

cases.title: Vidya Charitable Trust v. Desai
cases.facts:
The Vidya Charitable Trust was established in 1980 by a philanthropist to
run a free hospital for the underprivileged in a rural district. The
trust deed explicitly stated the trust property could never be sold or
used for commercial gain. Mr. Desai, a prominent local businessman, was
appointed as the Managing Trustee in 2015. In 2023, noticing that the
land surrounding the hospital had skyrocketed in value due to a new
highway, Desai orchestrated a scheme. Without informing the Charity
Commissioner or the other trustees, Desai leased 5 acres of the vacant
trust land on a 99-year lease to "Sunrise Developers," a private real
estate firm, for a fraction of the market rate.

It was later uncovered that Sunrise Developers was a shell company
secretly owned by Desai's son. Sunrise subsequently built a luxury
commercial complex on the land, generating massive personal wealth for
Desai's family. The other trustees discovered the fraud and filed a civil
suit under Section 92 of the Civil Procedure Code (CPC) and the Indian
Trusts Act, 1882, seeking the immediate removal of Desai, the
cancellation of the 99-year lease, and an accounting of all illicit
profits.
cases.issues:
Does the unauthorized leasing of charitable trust property to a
relative's company at an undervaluation constitute a gross breach of
fiduciary duty by a trustee?

Can a civil court cancel a registered 99-year commercial lease to a third
party (Sunrise) if it is proven to be the result of a fraudulent breach
of trust?

Under the Indian Trusts Act, is the trustee personally liable to disgorge
(return) all secret profits made by his family members arising from the
trust property?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Vidya Charitable Trust)
The Plaintiffs argued that a trustee holds a position of absolute,
uncompromised fiduciary trust. Relying on Sections 51 and 52 of the
Indian Trusts Act, they argued that a trustee cannot use trust property
for his own profit, nor can he buy or lease trust property for himself or
his relatives without strict judicial permission. Desai's actions were a
textbook case of self-dealing and conflict of interest. Because the lease
was explicitly prohibited by the trust deed and executed mala fide to
enrich his own son, the lease is void ab initio. The Trust demanded the
piercing of the corporate veil of "Sunrise Developers" and the
disgorgement of all commercial rents collected, asserting that equity
will not allow a fiduciary to profit from his own fraud.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Desai & Sunrise Developers)
Desai argued a technical defense. He claimed the hospital was running out
of funds, and the lease was a bona fide business decision to generate
steady income for the charity. He argued that Sunrise Developers is a
separate legal entity, and the fact that his son was a shareholder did
not legally equate to "self-dealing." Sunrise Developers argued that they
were a bona fide third-party purchaser for value without notice of the
internal trust deed restrictions. Therefore, the registered 99-year lease
could not be cancelled without causing them immense commercial damage,
and the Trust's remedy was merely to seek damages from Desai, not the
cancellation of the property rights.
cases.judgment:
The District Court, exercising its special jurisdiction under Section 92
CPC, ruled overwhelmingly in favor of the Vidya Charitable Trust. Desai
was immediately removed as trustee. The 99-year lease to Sunrise
Developers was cancelled and declared void. Desai and his son were
ordered to disgorge all illicit profits made from the commercial complex
back into the Trust's accounts. The Plaintiffs prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a scorching condemnation of fiduciary corruption. The
judge applied the strict equitable principles of the Indian Trusts Act. A
trustee has an absolute duty of loyalty. The Court pierced the veil of
Sunrise Developers, ruling that the company was a mere alter-ego used by
Desai to circumvent the rule against self-dealing.

The Court summarily dismissed the "bona fide purchaser" defense. Because
Sunrise was controlled by Desai's son, the company had full "constructive
notice" of the trust deed's prohibitions. You cannot be a bona fide
purchaser of a fraud you helped orchestrate. The Court ruled that any
transaction where a trustee alienates trust property for the direct or
indirect benefit of their own family is inherently tainted and voidable
at the option of the beneficiaries. Applying the doctrine of Constructive
Trust, the Court ruled that all the commercial profits generated by the
luxury complex legally belonged to the charity, as they were the fruits
of a poisoned tree. Equity demands the absolute disgorgement of secret
profits to strip the fiduciary of any incentive to breach their trust.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case vehemently enforces the Rule against Self-Dealing and Breach of
Fiduciary Duty (Indian Trusts Act, 1882). It establishes the absolute
equitable principle that a trustee cannot directly or indirectly alienate
trust property to benefit themselves or their relatives. Any such
transaction is voidable, and courts will actively pierce the corporate
veil and order absolute disgorgement of secret profits back to the
charitable trust.

cases.title: Global Tech GmbH v. IndiaSys Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Global Tech GmbH, a German software conglomerate, entered into a
technology transfer agreement with IndiaSys Pvt. Ltd. The contract was
governed by German law, with the seat of arbitration in Geneva,
Switzerland. A severe dispute arose when IndiaSys allegedly stole the
proprietary source code and began selling it under their own name. Global
Tech initiated arbitration in Geneva. IndiaSys participated but
eventually walked out of the proceedings, claiming the arbitrator was
biased. The Geneva tribunal proceeded ex parte and issued a massive
arbitral award of €50 Million against IndiaSys for intellectual property
theft and breach of contract.

Global Tech approached the Delhi High Court under Part II of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, seeking to enforce the Geneva
award against IndiaSys's assets in India. IndiaSys fiercely opposed the
enforcement under Section 48 of the Act, arguing that the award was
obtained without giving them a fair hearing (violating natural justice)
and that enforcing an award for massive, "punitive" damages for IP theft
violates the "Fundamental Public Policy of India."
cases.issues:
Under Section 48 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, can an
Indian court refuse to enforce a foreign arbitral award on the grounds
that the damages awarded are exorbitant and allegedly "punitive"?

Does an ex parte foreign award violate the principles of natural justice
if the defaulting party voluntarily walked out of the arbitration
proceedings?

What is the precise threshold for defining the "Fundamental Public Policy
of India" as a defense to resist the execution of a foreign arbitral
award?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Global Tech GmbH - Award
Creditor)
Global Tech argued for the pro-enforcement bias of the New York
Convention and the Indian Arbitration Act. Relying on landmark judgments
like Renusagar Power Co. Ltd. v. General Electric Co. and Vijay Karia v.
Prysmian Cavi E Sistemi, they argued that the grounds to refuse a foreign
award are incredibly narrow. They asserted that IndiaSys voluntarily
abandoned the Geneva proceedings; therefore, they cannot claim a denial
of natural justice. Furthermore, Global Tech argued that the "Public
Policy" exception cannot be used as an excuse to re-litigate the merits
of the case. The damages were compensatory for the massive global theft
of IP, not punitive, and enforcing contracts and punishing IP theft is
exactly in line with Indian public policy, not against it.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (IndiaSys - Award Debtor)
IndiaSys argued that enforcing a €50 Million award would bankrupt an
Indian domestic company, leading to massive job losses, which is
detrimental to the national economic interest and thus against public
policy. They argued that Indian contract law does not generally permit
astronomical punitive damages (Section 74 of the Contract Act), and
enforcing a Swiss award that functions like a punitive fine violates the
fundamental ethos of Indian jurisprudence. They further maintained that
the Swiss arbitrator exhibited bias, forcing them to walk out, meaning
the award was passed in violation of the sacred principle of Audi Alteram
Partem (right to a fair hearing).
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court ruled in favor of Global Tech GmbH. The Court
dismissed IndiaSys's objections under Section 48 and ordered the
execution and enforcement of the €50 Million Geneva arbitral award
against IndiaSys's assets. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment heavily reinforcing India's status as a
pro-arbitration jurisdiction. The judge strictly interpreted Section 48
of the Act, ruling that an enforcing court cannot act as an appellate
court to review the merits, facts, or quantum of damages of a foreign
award.

Addressing the "Natural Justice" argument, the Court found that IndiaSys
was given ample notice and opportunity to present its case in Geneva.
Voluntarily walking out of a legally convened arbitration is a strategic
choice, not a denial of natural justice by the tribunal. You cannot
abandon a match and then complain you weren't allowed to play.

Most critically, the Court dismantled the "Public Policy" defense. The
judge reaffirmed that "Fundamental Public Policy of India" is an
exceptionally high threshold. It refers to the most basic notions of
morality and justice. The Court ruled that protecting intellectual
property and penalizing blatant corporate theft is the cornerstone of
global commerce and Indian law. The fact that the damages were
exceptionally high or would bankrupt the defendant does not make the
award contrary to public policy. Indian courts will not refuse
enforcement merely because a foreign tribunal interpreted a contract or
calculated damages differently than an Indian court might have.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case critically reinforces the Pro-Enforcement Bias of Foreign
Arbitral Awards (Part II, Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996). It
establishes the rigid legal principle that the "Public Policy of India"
exception under Section 48 is exceptionally narrow. Courts will not
review the merits or quantum of damages of a foreign award, and a party
cannot claim a violation of natural justice if they voluntarily abandoned
the foreign proceedings.

cases.title: Sharma v. Dr. Gupta
cases.facts:
Mrs. Sharma, aged 45, was admitted to a private hospital under the care
of Dr. Gupta, a senior gynecologist, for a routine laparoscopic
appendectomy. Prior to the surgery, Mrs. Sharma signed a standard consent
form authorizing the appendectomy and "any other procedure deemed
necessary in the course of the operation." While she was under general
anesthesia, Dr. Gupta discovered multiple large, benign fibroids in her
uterus. Believing that these fibroids would cause her significant pain in
the future and require a second surgery, Dr. Gupta unilaterally decided
to perform a total hysterectomy (removal of the uterus) alongside the
appendectomy. There was no immediate, life-threatening emergency
necessitating the hysterectomy. Upon waking and discovering she had been
permanently deprived of her reproductive organs without her explicit
prior consent, Mrs. Sharma filed a civil suit for medical battery,
negligence, and severe mental trauma.
cases.issues:
Does a blanket consent form covering "any other necessary procedure"
legally authorize a surgeon to perform a major, non-emergency organ
removal?

What is the legal standard for "Informed Consent" in Indian medical
jurisprudence?

Did Dr. Gupta's actions constitute medical negligence or the civil tort
of battery?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mrs. Sharma)
The Plaintiff argued that the removal of her uterus was an unconsented,
catastrophic invasion of her bodily autonomy. Relying on the Supreme
Court's landmark judgment in Samira Kohli v. Dr. Prabha Manchanda, she
asserted that consent given for a specific diagnostic or surgical
procedure does not extend to an entirely different, major surgery unless
there is an imminent threat to life. Since the fibroids were benign and
posed no immediate danger, Dr. Gupta had an absolute legal duty to close
the incision, wake the patient, and seek her informed, explicit consent
for the hysterectomy. The Plaintiff argued this unauthorized amputation
amounted to civil battery and a gross violation of her fundamental right
to privacy and bodily integrity.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Dr. Gupta)
The Defendant argued that he acted in the utmost good faith and in the
best clinical interest of the patient. He contended that the blanket
consent form legally empowered him to make intra-operative decisions to
spare the patient the physical trauma, surgical risk, and financial
burden of a second, inevitable surgery under general anesthesia. He
relied on the traditional Bolam test, arguing that a substantial body of
medical professionals would agree that removing painful fibroids when
already operating in the pelvic region is a sound clinical practice.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court ruled in favor of Mrs. Sharma. Dr. Gupta and the hospital
were held jointly liable for medical battery and deficiency in service,
and were ordered to pay substantial compensatory damages. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly applied the Samira Kohli precedent, delivering a
decisive victory for patient autonomy over medical paternalism. The judge
ruled that the traditional Bolam test (what doctors think is best) does
not govern the realm of consent. Indian law requires "real and valid
consent," which necessitates the patient being informed of the nature,
risks, and alternatives of a specific procedure. The Court held that a
pre-printed, blanket consent form is legally void as it lacks
specificity. Because the fibroids were benign and not life-threatening,
no medical emergency justified bypassing the patient's right to choose.
The Court reasoned that a surgeon cannot substitute their own judgment
for the patient's bodily autonomy. The unauthorized removal of an organ,
regardless of the doctor's benevolent intentions, constitutes the tort of
battery.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the doctrine of Informed Consent in Medical
Jurisprudence. It establishes the legal principle that a surgeon cannot
perform an unauthorized, non-emergency procedure based on a blanket
consent form or paternalistic "good faith." Doing so constitutes Medical
Battery and a gross violation of the patient's bodily autonomy.

cases.title: BuildCorp India v. State Infrastructure Board
cases.facts:
BuildCorp India entered into a government contract with the State
Infrastructure Board to construct a 50-kilometer highway. The total
contract value was ₹500 Crores, with a completion deadline of 36 months.
Clause 14 of the contract stated: "In the event of any delay beyond the
stipulated completion date, the contractor shall be liable to pay a
penalty of ₹1 Crore per day of delay." Due to severe, unseasonal monsoons
and a subsequent labor strike, BuildCorp delayed the completion by 60
days. The State Board withheld ₹60 Crores from the final payment, citing
Clause 14. BuildCorp sued the Board, arguing that the actual loss caused
to the State by the 60-day delay was negligible (as the connecting bridge
was also unfinished), and the ₹60 Crore deduction was an illegal,
unconscionable penalty rather than a genuine pre-estimate of damages.
cases.issues:
Is a clause explicitly stipulating a massive per-day fine for delay
enforceable as Liquidated Damages, or is it void as an in terrorem
Penalty?

Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, is the aggrieved party
required to prove actual, quantifiable loss to claim the stipulated
amount?

Can the State enforce a draconian penalty clause if the delay caused no
actual commercial detriment?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (BuildCorp India)
The Plaintiff argued that Indian contract law prohibits punitive damages
for breach of contract. Relying on Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi
Development Authority, BuildCorp argued that Section 74 dictates that
only "reasonable compensation" can be awarded, up to the maximum
stipulated limit. The ₹1 Crore per day clause was clearly drafted in
terrorem to frighten the contractor into performance, not as a genuine,
calculated pre-estimate of loss. Because the connecting infrastructure
was delayed anyway, the State suffered zero actual loss from BuildCorp's
60-day delay. Therefore, withholding ₹60 Crores was unjust enrichment.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State Infrastructure Board)
The Defendant argued that BuildCorp, a massive commercial entity, signed
the contract with full awareness of the delay clause. They argued that in
complex public infrastructure projects, quantifying exact financial loss
(public inconvenience, delayed economic development) is impossible.
Therefore, the sum stipulated in the contract should be recognized as a
genuine pre-estimate of liquidated damages agreed upon by two
sophisticated commercial parties. The Board argued that the courts should
not rewrite commercial contracts to rescue a defaulting party from a bad
bargain.
cases.judgment:
The Commercial Court ruled in favor of BuildCorp India. The Court struck
down the ₹60 Crore deduction as an illegal penalty, ordering the State
Board to release the funds, allowing them to retain only a nominal sum
for administrative delays. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a masterclass on Section 74 of the Contract Act. The
judge ruled that merely labeling a clause "Liquidated Damages" does not
make it so; the court must examine the substance. A sum is a penalty if
it is extravagant and unconscionable compared to the greatest conceivable
loss that could follow the breach. ₹1 Crore a day was deemed
astronomically disproportionate.

Furthermore, the Court clarified the evidentiary burden under Section 74.
While a party doesn't have to prove exact mathematical loss if it's
impossible to calculate, they must prove that they suffered some legal
injury or loss. Since the State could not open the highway anyway due to
the unfinished bridge, they suffered zero operational or financial
detriment from BuildCorp's delay. The Court held that enforcing the ₹60
Crore deduction would violate the compensatory nature of Indian contract
law, turning a civil breach into a massive, unjustified windfall for the
State.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case firmly distinguishes between Liquidated Damages and Penalties
under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. It establishes the
legal principle that extravagant, unconscionable delay clauses intended
as a threat are void as penalties, and courts will only award reasonable
compensation based on actual or probable legal injury, forbidding unjust
enrichment from a victimless breach.

cases.title: Singh v. Kapoor Estate
cases.facts:
In 1990, Mr. Kapoor, a wealthy NRI, hired Ram Singh as a caretaker and
watchman for his sprawling, 5-acre vacant ancestral property in Punjab.
Mr. Kapoor built a small outhouse on the property for Singh to live in
rent-free in exchange for keeping squatters away. For 30 years, Mr.
Kapoor rarely visited, only occasionally sending money for minor repairs.
Singh lived on the land, grew vegetables for his own use, and paid the
electricity bills in his own name. In 2025, Mr. Kapoor's heirs returned
to India to sell the land and asked Singh to vacate. Singh refused and
filed a civil suit seeking a declaration of title, claiming he had become
the absolute owner of the property through "Adverse Possession," having
occupied it continuously, openly, and uninterrupted for over 12 years.
cases.issues:
Can a caretaker, servant, or agent claim ownership of an employer's
property through the doctrine of Adverse Possession?

What is the legal distinction between permissive possession and hostile
(adverse) possession under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963?

Does paying utility bills and cultivating the land convert permissive
occupancy into an adverse claim of title?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Ram Singh)
The Plaintiff argued that 30 years of continuous, uninterrupted, and open
possession fulfills the statutory requirements of the Limitation Act. He
argued that the Kapoor family effectively abandoned the property. By
growing his own crops, paying the electricity bills in his name, and
holding himself out as the master of the land to the local community for
three decades, his possession became inherently hostile to the original
owners. He argued that the owners slept on their rights for 30 years and
lost their title.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Kapoor Estate)
The Defendants relied heavily on the Supreme Court ruling in Maria
Margarida Sequeira Fernandes v. Erasmo Jack de Sequeira. They argued that
Singh's entry onto the land was strictly permissive-he was an employee
placed there specifically to guard it. A caretaker holds the property on
behalf of the master. The defense argued that permissive possession, no
matter how long it lasts, can never automatically ripen into adverse
possession. Unless Singh committed a clear, overt act fundamentally
renouncing his status as a caretaker and explicitly declaring hostile
ownership to the true owners, his possession remained permissive. Paying
utility bills is a mere convenience, not an assertion of hostile title.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court dismissed Ram Singh's suit and ordered him to vacate the
premises immediately, granting possession back to the Kapoor Estate. The
Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court strictly defined the demanding threshold for adverse
possession. The judge ruled that the foundation of adverse possession is
animus possidendi-the specific, hostile intent to possess the land in
direct defiance of the true owner's rights. The Court held that a
caretaker, servant, or permissive tenant enters the land acknowledging
the superior title of the owner.

To convert permissive possession into adverse possession, the occupant
must commit a notorious, explicit act of ouster, making the true owner
undeniably aware that their title is being challenged. Merely living
there quietly for 30 years, paying bills, and growing vegetables are acts
consistent with the life of a caretaker. The Court ruled that an agent
cannot secretly usurp the principal's property. Because Singh never
explicitly communicated a hostile takeover to Mr. Kapoor, his possession
remained legally permissive for all 30 years, meaning the 12-year
statutory clock for adverse possession never even began ticking.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a rigid boundary against land-grabbing via the Doctrine of
Adverse Possession (Article 65, Limitation Act). It establishes the
absolute legal principle that possession by a caretaker, servant, or
agent is fundamentally permissive and can never ripen into adverse
possession without a clear, overt, and communicated act of hostile ouster
against the true owner.

cases.title: MakeMyTours v. Global Trip Planners
cases.facts:
"MakeMyTours" is a massive, highly recognized Indian online travel agency
holding a registered trademark for its name. In 2025, a smaller rival
company, "Global Trip Planners," initiated an aggressive digital
marketing campaign on a major search engine. Global Trip Planners
secretly bid on the keyword "MakeMyTours" in the search engine's ad
network. Consequently, whenever a consumer typed "MakeMyTours" into the
search bar, the very first "Sponsored Link" at the top of the page
directed the user to Global Trip Planners' website, often accompanied by
text like "Looking for Tours? Book with us for 50% less." MakeMyTours
sued Global Trip Planners and the Search Engine for Trademark
Infringement and Passing Off, demanding an immediate injunction.
cases.issues:
Does the invisible use of a competitor's registered trademark as a
"keyword" in a search engine advertising algorithm constitute Trademark
Infringement under Section 29 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999?

Does keyword bidding create "initial interest confusion" among consumers,
amounting to the tort of Passing Off?

Can the Search Engine be held liable as a contributory infringer for
selling trademarked keywords to third parties?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (MakeMyTours)
The Plaintiff argued that bidding on a competitor's trademark is a
digital hijacking of their brand equity. Relying on evolving digital IP
jurisprudence (like the MakeMyTrip v. Booking.com Delhi High Court
observations), they argued that utilizing their mark in the backend
algorithm to trigger a rival's ad is "use" in the course of trade under
Section 29. They argued this practice creates "initial interest
confusion." Even if the consumer realizes they are on a rival's website
after clicking, the rival has already unlawfully diverted traffic and
usurped the plaintiff's goodwill by using their trademark as bait.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Global Trip Planners & Search
Engine)
The Defendants argued that the trademark "MakeMyTours" was not visibly
used on Global Trip Planners' website or in the text of the ad itself. It
was only used in the invisible backend code. They argued that keyword
bidding fosters healthy market competition by showing consumers
alternatives. They asserted that modern internet users are sophisticated
enough to distinguish between a "Sponsored Ad" and an organic search
result, meaning there is no actual confusion regarding the source of the
services. The Search Engine claimed safe harbor protection as a mere
intermediary that does not initiate the transmission.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of MakeMyTours. The Court granted an
injunction prohibiting Global Trip Planners from bidding on the
trademarked keyword and ordered the Search Engine to restrict the sale of
the specific trademark as an ad word. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a critical update to trademark law for the digital
economy. The judge ruled that the definition of "use" under the Trade
Marks Act is not limited to physical or visible branding. Utilizing a
registered trademark in the backend algorithm to trigger commercial
advertising constitutes "use in the course of trade."

The Court heavily relied on the doctrine of "Initial Interest Confusion."
The judge reasoned that when a consumer searches for a specific brand,
their intent is to find that brand. By intercepting that search and
displaying a rival link at the very top, the defendant unlawfully free-
rides on the goodwill of the trademark owner. Even if the confusion is
dispelled later, the initial diversion of the customer is an act of
Passing Off. The Court held that a trademark is a valuable property
right, and selling it as a keyword allows competitors to siphon brand
equity, which is illegal.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case modernizes the Trade Marks Act, 1999 for the era of algorithmic
advertising. It establishes the legal principle that bidding on a
competitor's registered trademark as a search engine "keyword"
constitutes invisible Trademark Infringement and Passing Off, as it
unlawfully creates Initial Interest Confusion to divert consumer traffic.

cases.title: Desai v. The Daily Chronicle
cases.facts:
Vikram Desai is the highly visible CEO of a major Indian public sector
bank, widely praised for his anti-corruption stance. In September 2025,
The Daily Chronicle, a national investigative newspaper, published a
front-page article titled "The Hypocrite Banker." The article leaked
highly private, legally obtained WhatsApp chats between Desai and his
mistress, revealing a long-standing extramarital affair. The article did
not allege any financial corruption or misuse of bank funds; it solely
exposed his personal infidelity to highlight a "moral deficit" in his
character. Desai sued the newspaper for Defamation and a gross violation
of his Right to Privacy, demanding massive damages and a gag order.
cases.issues:
Does the publication of truthful, yet highly private and intimate
information about a public figure constitute the tort of Defamation or an
actionable Invasion of Privacy?

How does the Court balance a public figure's fundamental Right to Privacy
(Article 21) against the Freedom of the Press (Article 19(1)(a))?

Does the "public interest" defense apply to the exposure of a public
official's private sexual morality if it has no nexus to their official
duties?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Vikram Desai)
The Plaintiff argued relying heavily on the K.S. Puttaswamy (Right to
Privacy) judgment. He conceded the chats were real (defeating the
defamation claim, as truth is an absolute defense), but argued a severe
breach of informational privacy. He argued that his sexual orientation
and private relationships are the core of his human dignity. As a bank
CEO, his public duties involve financial regulation, not moral policing.
Because the affair had zero bearing on the bank's finances or his
professional competence, the publication served absolutely no legitimate
"public interest." It was pure, malicious voyeurism designed to destroy
his family and reputation for newspaper sales.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (The Daily Chronicle)
The Defendant newspaper anchored its defense in Freedom of the Press.
They argued that Desai, by positioning himself as an anti-corruption
crusader and moral leader of a public institution, had voluntarily thrust
himself into the public eye, thereby waiving a significant portion of his
privacy rights. They argued the "public interest" is not limited to
financial corruption; the public has a right to know if a high-ranking
public servant is a hypocrite operating with moral duplicity. They
asserted that gagging truthful reporting about powerful figures creates a
chilling effect on investigative journalism.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Vikram Desai on the grounds of Invasion
of Privacy, granting a permanent injunction against further publication
of the private chats and awarding substantial damages. The Defamation
claim was dismissed. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a nuanced judgment establishing the boundaries of
media reporting on public figures. The judge dismissed the defamation
claim immediately, affirming that truth is an absolute defense to civil
defamation. However, the Court came down heavily on the privacy
violation. Applying the Puttaswamy proportionality test, the Court
analyzed whether the breach of privacy served a legitimate, overriding
public interest.

The judge ruled that there is a massive legal distinction between "what
is in the public interest" and "what the public is merely interested in."
Prurient gossip about an affair is the latter. Because Desai's infidelity
involved no illegality, no misuse of public funds, and no conflict of
interest with his banking duties, his private sexual life remained
strictly within his zone of autonomy. The Court held that holding public
office does not strip a citizen of their fundamental human dignity. The
press cannot use the shield of Article 19(1)(a) to publish non-
consensual, intimate data that serves no democratic purpose other than
sensationalist character assassination.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case delineates the boundary between the Right to Privacy (Article
21) and Freedom of the Press (Article 19(1)(a)). It establishes the legal
principle that truthful publication of intimate, private information
constitutes an actionable Invasion of Privacy if the information lacks a
strict, legitimate nexus to the public figure's official duties,
confirming that public curiosity does not equate to "public interest."

cases.title: Apex Infrastructure v. State Bank of India
cases.facts:
Apex Infrastructure entered into a contract to build a stadium for a
State Sports Authority. As per standard commercial practice, Apex
provided an "Unconditional Bank Guarantee" of ₹20 Crores issued by the
State Bank of India (SBI) in favor of the Sports Authority, to secure
performance. Midway through the project, a massive dispute arose over
design changes. The Sports Authority, claiming Apex was in breach,
immediately wrote to SBI to invoke the ₹20 Crore bank guarantee. Apex
filed an urgent civil suit seeking an injunction to stop SBI from paying
out the guarantee, claiming the Sports Authority was executing a massive,
retaliatory fraud, as Apex had actually completed 80% of the work and the
Authority was trying to bankrupt them to avoid paying the final bills.
cases.issues:
Under what specific, exceptional circumstances can a civil court grant an
injunction restraining the encashment of an "Unconditional Bank
Guarantee"?

Does a contractual dispute regarding the percentage of work completed
justify halting the invocation of a bank guarantee?

What constitutes "egregious fraud" or "irretrievable injustice" in the
context of commercial bank guarantees?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Infrastructure)
The Plaintiff argued that allowing the Sports Authority to encash ₹20
Crores when 80% of the work was already certified by independent
engineers constituted an egregious, malicious fraud. They argued that the
encashment was a pressure tactic. Relying on exceptions recognized in
Indian commercial law, Apex argued that losing ₹20 Crores instantly would
completely bankrupt their company, resulting in "special equities" and
"irretrievable injustice." They argued the court must intervene to
prevent the Sports Authority from unjustly enriching themselves while the
underlying contractual dispute is pending arbitration.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Sports Authority & SBI)
SBI argued that an Unconditional Bank Guarantee is an independent
contract between the Bank and the Beneficiary. The bank is legally
obligated to pay upon demand, without questioning the underlying dispute
between the contractor and the authority. The Sports Authority relied on
landmark precedents like U.P. State Sugar Corporation v. Sumac
International Ltd., asserting that courts should virtually never
interfere with bank guarantees, as doing so destroys the entire
foundation of commercial trust and liquidity. They argued that Apex's
claims of 80% completion are mere contractual disputes, not "egregious
fraud," and Apex can claim the money back in arbitration if they win.
cases.judgment:
The Commercial Court refused to grant the injunction. The State Bank of
India was permitted to encash and transfer the ₹20 Crores to the Sports
Authority. The Defendants prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a rigid defense of commercial banking instruments.
The judge reiterated the absolute sanctity of an Unconditional Bank
Guarantee. The Court ruled that a bank guarantee is a distinct,
autonomous contract. The bank cannot, and the courts should not, inquire
into the underlying dispute between the parties regarding who breached
the construction contract.

The judge addressed the two narrow exceptions where an injunction is
permissible: (1) Fraud of an egregious nature that vitiates the entire
underlying transaction (e.g., the contract itself was forged), and (2)
Special Equities/Irretrievable Injustice. The Court ruled that a dispute
over the percentage of work completed is a standard breach of contract
issue, not an "egregious fraud." Furthermore, the threat of bankruptcy
for Apex does not constitute "irretrievable injustice," because if Apex
wins the arbitration, they can legally recover the ₹20 Crores from the
State Sports Authority. Therefore, halting the guarantee would
unjustifiably paralyze established mechanisms of commercial security.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case fiercely protects the Autonomy of Unconditional Bank
Guarantees. It cements the legal principle that courts will not grant
injunctions against the invocation of bank guarantees based on standard
contractual disputes. Injunctions are strictly limited to the rarest
cases of egregious, fundamental fraud or absolute irretrievable injustice
where recovery of the money would be legally impossible.

cases.title: Anjali v. Rajat
cases.facts:
Anjali and Rajat were married in 2010. By 2013, the marriage had
deteriorated into bitter, continuous litigation. They filed dozens of
civil and criminal cases against each other, including allegations of
cruelty and dowry harassment, all of which ended in acquittals or
settlements. They lived completely separately for 12 years. In 2025,
Rajat approached the Supreme Court, seeking a divorce on the grounds of
"Irretrievable Breakdown of Marriage." Anjali fiercely opposed the
divorce. She explicitly stated in court that she hated Rajat and would
never live with him again, but she refused to grant a mutual consent
divorce purely to punish him, vowing to keep him legally tied to her
forever.
cases.issues:
Is "Irretrievable Breakdown of Marriage" a recognized, statutory ground
for contested divorce under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955?

Can the Supreme Court utilize its inherent, extraordinary powers under
Article 142 of the Constitution to dissolve a dead marriage even if one
spouse explicitly refuses to consent?

How does the Court balance the sanctity of the marital statute against
the cruelty of maintaining a legally dead, vindictive marriage?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Rajat)
The Appellant relied heavily on the Constitution Bench judgment in Shilpa
Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan. Rajat argued that the marriage was a legal
fiction. They had lived apart for 12 years, destroyed each other with
litigation, and possessed zero emotional bond. He argued that forcing a
citizen to remain tethered to a vindictive spouse in a demonstrably dead
marriage violates his fundamental right to life and dignity under Article
21. Because the Hindu Marriage Act lacks a specific provision for
irretrievable breakdown without mutual consent, he pleaded with the
Supreme Court to invoke Article 142 to do "complete justice" and sever
the dead tie.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Anjali)
The Respondent argued a strict statutory defense. She pointed out that
the legislature has deliberately chosen not to amend the Hindu Marriage
Act to include "irretrievable breakdown" as a fault-less ground for
contested divorce. She argued that the Supreme Court should not usurp the
legislative function. She asserted her legal right to remain a married
woman and argued that granting Rajat a divorce without her consent
rewards him for abandoning the marriage and deprives her of her legal
status and future financial security as a wife.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Rajat. Bypassing the statutory
limitations of the Hindu Marriage Act, the Court invoked Article 142 of
the Constitution to formally dissolve the marriage on the grounds of its
irretrievable breakdown, while simultaneously ordering Rajat to pay a
massive, permanent alimony settlement to Anjali. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court delivered a pragmatic and empathetic judgment,
addressing a massive void in Indian family law. The Court acknowledged
that the Hindu Marriage Act does not statutorily recognize irretrievable
breakdown without mutual consent. However, the Court declared that it is
not powerless when faced with manifest injustice. Applying the Shilpa
Sailesh precedent, the Court ruled that Article 142 empowers the Supreme
Court to pass any decree necessary for doing "complete justice."

The Court analyzed the facts: 12 years of separation, relentless hostile
litigation, and the wife's explicit admission that she only stayed
married to punish the husband. The judge reasoned that a marriage is
built on companionship; when that is permanently destroyed, preserving
the legal shell of the marriage is an act of extreme mental cruelty to
both parties. The Court ruled that it will not force parties to endure
endless agony waiting for a legislative amendment. By granting the
divorce but securing Anjali's financial future with heavy alimony, the
Court achieved complete equitable justice.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case operationalizes the power of the Supreme Court regarding
Irretrievable Breakdown of Marriage. It establishes the vital principle
that the Supreme Court can invoke its extraordinary jurisdiction under
Article 142 of the Constitution to dissolve a fundamentally dead
marriage, bypassing the strict statutory requirement for mutual consent
under the Hindu Marriage Act to prevent ongoing mental cruelty.

cases.title: Green Valley Residents v. ChemDye Corp.
cases.facts:
ChemDye Corp operates a massive textile dyeing facility bordering the
Green Valley residential colony. For five years, to avoid the costs of
treating chemical effluent, ChemDye secretly pumped highly toxic,
untreated wastewater into deep, unlined borewells on their property. Over
time, these heavy metals seeped into the underground aquifer. In 2024,
residents of Green Valley began suffering from severe skin lesions and
gastrointestinal diseases. Independent testing revealed the colony's
groundwater was lethally toxic. The Residents Association filed a civil
suit before the National Green Tribunal (NGT), demanding absolute
liability, massive compensation, and the immediate closure of the
factory. ChemDye argued that the seepage was an invisible, underground
accident and they complied with surface environmental regulations.
cases.issues:
Is a corporation strictly and absolutely liable for underground aquifer
contamination caused by their industrial activities?

Does the "Polluter Pays" principle require the offending industry to
compensate victims and bear the entire cost of reversing the ecological
damage?

Can the NGT order the permanent closure of an economically significant
industry to protect public health?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Green Valley Residents)
The Plaintiffs relied on the doctrine of Absolute Liability established
in the Oleum Gas Leak Case (M.C. Mehta) and the Vellore Citizens Welfare
Forum judgment. They argued that operating a chemical dye factory is an
inherently dangerous and hazardous activity. Therefore, ChemDye holds an
