absolute, non-delegable duty to the community. Bypassing treatment plants
to pump toxins directly into the earth is a calculated, malicious
destruction of public resources. The Plaintiffs demanded the application
of the "Polluter Pays" principle, asserting that ChemDye must compensate
every sick resident and pay the hundreds of crores required to remediate
the groundwater.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (ChemDye Corp)
ChemDye Corp argued that they possessed all valid surface operational
licenses from the State Pollution Control Board. They contended that
groundwater hydrology is complex and unpredictable; the underground
migration of the chemicals was an unforeseeable accident, negating the
malicious intent required for punitive damages. They further argued that
shutting down the factory would result in the loss of 5,000 jobs,
devastating the local economy. They proposed paying a fine and installing
a water purification plant for the colony instead of facing a complete
shutdown and absolute liability.
cases.judgment:
The NGT ruled decisively in favor of the Green Valley Residents. The
Tribunal ordered the immediate and permanent closure of the ChemDye
facility, seized their corporate assets, and ordered them to pay massive
compensation to the victims and fund a state-led aquifer remediation
project. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Tribunal delivered a crushing verdict rooted in absolute
environmental accountability. The judge applied the Precautionary
Principle and the Polluter Pays principle. The NGT ruled that deep-well
injection of untreated toxic effluent is not an "accident"; it is a
deliberate, clandestine method of illegal waste disposal. Following the
Absolute Liability doctrine, the Court held that industries engaged in
hazardous activities owe an absolute duty to the community; if harm
occurs-even underground and out of sight-the enterprise is absolutely
liable to compensate, regardless of whether they took "reasonable care"
on the surface.

The Court summarily dismissed the economic argument regarding job losses.
The judge stated that "Sustainable Development" does not mean tolerating
the poisoning of citizens for corporate profit. The Right to Clean Water
is an integral part of the Right to Life (Article 21). The Court held
that an industry that cannot operate without destroying the foundational
ecology of its surroundings has no legal right to exist.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case vigorously enforces the Doctrine of Absolute Liability and the
Polluter Pays Principle in environmental torts. It establishes that
industries are absolutely and exclusively liable for insidious ecological
damage like groundwater contamination, and courts will prioritize the
Constitutional Right to a Clean Environment (Article 21) by permanently
shutting down polluting enterprises, disregarding economic or employment
defenses.

cases.title: Sharma v. MegaMart Online
cases.facts:
Mr. Sharma purchased a high-end "Flash-Charge" mobile power bank from
"MegaMart Online," India's largest e-commerce marketplace. The product
listing prominently displayed the "MegaMart Assured" badge, promising
quality checks. The power bank was manufactured and sold by a third-party
vendor located in China, using MegaMart's platform. Two weeks later,
while charging on Sharma's nightstand, the power bank suffered a
catastrophic thermal runaway, exploding and causing a severe fire that
destroyed his bedroom and caused him third-degree burns. Sharma sued
MegaMart Online for product liability, deficiency in service, and massive
compensation under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
cases.issues:
Can an e-commerce marketplace be held liable under "Product Liability"
for a defective product sold by a third-party vendor on its platform?

Does the use of a proprietary quality assurance badge (e.g., "MegaMart
Assured") strip the e-commerce platform of its "Intermediary Safe Harbor"
protection under the Information Technology Act?

Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, what are the distinct
liabilities of a product seller versus an electronic service provider?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. Sharma)
The Plaintiff anchored his case in the robust provisions of the Consumer
Protection Act, 2019, which specifically includes e-commerce. He argued
that he did not buy the product from an unknown Chinese vendor; he
trusted the reputation, the payment gateway, and the delivery logistics
of MegaMart. Crucially, he argued that by placing a "MegaMart Assured"
badge on the listing, the platform actively endorsed the safety and
quality of the product, thereby stepping out of its passive role as a
mere digital noticeboard. Therefore, MegaMart must be held jointly and
strictly liable as a "Product Seller" for selling a lethally defective
product.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (MegaMart Online)
MegaMart relied heavily on Section 79 of the Information Technology Act,
claiming absolute "Intermediary Safe Harbor" immunity. They argued they
are merely a technological bridge connecting independent buyers and
sellers. They do not manufacture, inspect, or own the inventory of third-
party sellers. They argued that the "Assured" badge only relates to fast
shipping and basic packaging checks, not deep metallurgical safety
testing of electronic components. They contended that Sharma's sole legal
remedy was against the Chinese manufacturer, and holding platforms liable
for millions of third-party products would destroy the e-commerce
industry in India.
cases.judgment:
The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) ruled in
favor of Mr. Sharma. MegaMart Online was denied intermediary immunity and
ordered to pay substantial compensation for the physical injuries and
property damage. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Commission delivered a critical judgment interpreting e-commerce
liability under the 2019 Act. The NCDRC acknowledged the IT Act's Safe
Harbor provision but ruled it is not an absolute shield against consumer
protection laws. The judge scrutinized the operational reality of the
transaction. Because MegaMart controlled the payment, the return policy,
the delivery, and most importantly, applied an "Assured" badge of
quality, they were not a passive, neutral intermediary.

The Commission ruled that the "Assured" badge creates a legitimate
expectation of safety in the mind of the consumer. By actively vouching
for the product, MegaMart transitioned into the role of a "Product
Seller" under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. The Court held that
massive e-commerce platforms cannot reap billions in commissions while
completely disowning the safety of the products they heavily promote and
deliver. If they utilize trust-badges to drive sales, they assume a
concurrent, strict product liability for catastrophic defects.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a major precedent for E-Commerce Liability under the
Consumer Protection Act, 2019. It restricts the Intermediary Safe Harbor
(Section 79 IT Act), establishing the legal principle that when an e-
commerce platform actively vouches for a product's quality (e.g., via
"Assured" badges) and controls the transaction logistics, it assumes
strict Product Liability alongside the manufacturer for defective and
dangerous goods.

cases.title: Apex Commodities v. Delta Mills
cases.facts:
On September 1, 2024, Apex Commodities entered into a forward contract to
sell 10,000 bales of raw cotton to Delta Mills at ₹5,000 per bale, with
delivery and payment scheduled for December 1, 2024. On October 15, 2024,
the global price of cotton plummeted to ₹3,500 per bale. Realizing they
made a terrible bargain, Delta Mills immediately sent an unequivocal
email to Apex Commodities, repudiating the contract entirely and stating
they would refuse delivery.

Apex Commodities received this notice of anticipatory breach but chose to
ignore it. They did not sell the cotton in the open market in October.
Instead, they held onto the inventory, insisting the contract remained
alive. By the delivery date of December 1, the market had crashed further
to ₹2,000 per bale. Apex then sued Delta Mills for damages, claiming the
difference between the contract price (₹5,000) and the market price on
the date of delivery (₹2,000), amounting to a massive ₹3 Crore claim.
cases.issues:
Upon receiving a clear notice of anticipatory breach under Section 39 of
the Indian Contract Act, does the innocent party have an absolute legal
duty to mitigate their damages immediately?

If the innocent party chooses to keep the contract alive until the
delivery date, at what date should the market price be calculated to
determine the quantum of damages under Section 73?

Can Delta Mills be held liable for the additional market crash that
occurred after their clear repudiation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Commodities)
Apex argued that an anticipatory breach does not automatically terminate
the contract unless the innocent party accepts the repudiation. Relying
on the doctrine of election, Apex argued they had the absolute legal
right to keep the contract alive until the specified performance date
(December 1). They contended that Delta Mills could have changed their
mind and accepted the delivery. Therefore, damages must be strictly
calculated based on the market price on the date the performance was
actually due, making Delta liable for the entire ₹3 Crore loss.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Delta Mills)
Delta Mills argued that Section 73 imposes a strict, unavoidable duty on
the plaintiff to mitigate their losses. They asserted that Apex acted
vindictively by holding the cotton in a crashing market instead of
selling it reasonably in October. Delta argued that if Apex had accepted
the breach in October, the damages would only be the difference between
₹5,000 and ₹3,500. They contended that they cannot be held financially
responsible for the plaintiff's stubborn refusal to mitigate losses over
the subsequent six weeks.
cases.judgment:
The Commercial Court ruled in favor of Apex Commodities regarding the
breach, but severely restricted the quantum of damages awarded. The Court
calculated damages based on the market price on the date of delivery
(December 1), but deducted the amount Apex could have saved through
mitigation. The Defendant partially prevailed on the damages calculation.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a precise analysis of Section 39 and Section 73 of
the Contract Act. The judge affirmed that Apex had the right to ignore
the anticipatory breach and keep the contract alive. Consequently, the
breach technically occurred on December 1, and damages are calculated
based on the market price on that day.

However, the Court came down heavily on the duty to mitigate. The judge
ruled that the right to keep the contract alive does not grant the
plaintiff a license to deliberately aggravate their financial injury. The
law does not reward commercial absurdity. While the date of calculation
remains December 1, the Court applied the "Mitigation Principle" from the
Explanation to Section 73. Apex had a duty to act as a prudent commercial
entity. A reasonable entity would have executed a substitute forward
contract in October when the price was ₹3,500. Because Apex failed to
take reasonable steps to mitigate, the Court only awarded damages
equating to the loss they would have suffered had they mitigated in
October.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case firmly establishes the interaction between Anticipatory Breach
(Section 39) and the Duty to Mitigate Damages (Section 73). It sets the
legal principle that while an innocent party may elect to keep a
repudiated contract alive until the performance date, they cannot claim
compensation for any aggravated losses that could have been avoided
through reasonable commercial mitigation.

cases.title: Sharma v. State Revenue Authority
cases.facts:
In 2022, to spur industrial development in a highly impoverished,
drought-prone district, the State Government issued a formal, gazetted
industrial policy. The policy explicitly promised a 10-year total
exemption from State Goods and Services Tax (SGST) for any heavy
manufacturing plant established in the district before 2024. Relying
entirely on this unequivocal sovereign promise, Mr. Sharma took a massive
loan, purchased barren land, and constructed a ₹100 Crore steel
manufacturing plant, completing it in late 2023.

In January 2025, facing a severe state budget deficit, the newly elected
State Government unilaterally revoked the industrial policy, citing
"overriding public interest and revenue constraints." They issued tax
demand notices to Mr. Sharma. He filed a writ petition in the High Court,
invoking the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel, demanding the State honor
its 10-year tax holiday.
cases.issues:
Can the equitable doctrine of Promissory Estoppel be enforced against the
State or Government authorities acting in their sovereign, legislative
capacity?

Does a change in government or a state revenue deficit constitute an
"overriding public interest" sufficient to retroactively break a gazetted
economic promise?

Under what circumstances can the State unilaterally alter its tax
exemption policies without compensating parties who altered their
position based on those policies?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. Sharma)
Mr. Sharma anchored his case in the landmark Supreme Court judgment
Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills v. State of UP. He argued that the doctrine
of Promissory Estoppel is a sword of equity against state arbitrariness.
The State made a clear, unequivocal representation meant to be acted
upon. Sharma altered his financial position detrimentally (investing ₹100
Crores) relying exclusively on that promise. He argued that allowing the
State to unilaterally renege on its promises destroys commercial trust
and completely violates Article 14 (protection against arbitrary state
action).

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State Revenue Authority)
The State argued that Promissory Estoppel cannot curtail the sovereign,
legislative power of taxation. They relied on cases like Kasinka Trading
v. Union of India, asserting that tax exemptions are a matter of
executive policy, not binding commercial contracts. The State contended
that the severe budget deficit threatened basic public services
(healthcare, sanitation), constituting a supervening, overriding public
interest. The government cannot be indefinitely paralyzed by the promises
of a previous administration if enforcing them would bankrupt the state
exchequer.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mr. Sharma. The Court struck down the
retroactive tax demands and ordered the State to honor the SGST exemption
for the remainder of the 10-year period for plants established before the
revocation. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a robust defense of equitable estoppel against
administrative arbitrariness. The judge acknowledged that the State has
the power to change its policies prospectively. However, the Court
strictly applied the Motilal Padampat test. To defeat promissory
estoppel, the State must prove an absolute, compelling "supervening
public interest" that makes it highly inequitable to hold them to the
promise.

The Court ruled that a mere budget deficit or a desire to collect more
revenue does not constitute an overriding public equity. The State knew
the financial implications when it issued the policy. Inducing a citizen
to invest ₹100 Crores in a barren district and then immediately pulling
the financial rug out from under them is grossly arbitrary and violates
Article 14. The Court held that the government's word must carry
sanctity. While the State can cancel the policy for future investors,
they are strictly estopped from reneging on the promise to those who have
already irretrievably altered their position in reliance upon it.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case heavily reinforces the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel against
the State. It establishes the legal principle that while the government
can alter prospective tax policies, it cannot retroactively renege on
specific, gazetted promises of tax holidays upon which citizens have
detrimentally relied, unless it proves a catastrophic, supervening public
emergency far beyond mere revenue shortfalls.

cases.title: Neha v. Rahul
cases.facts:
Neha and Rahul were married in 2018. Neha holds a Master's degree in
Business Administration (MBA) from a premier institute and worked as a
high-level marketing executive earning ₹2 Lakhs per month. In 2023, the
marriage broke down due to ideological differences, and they separated.
Neha voluntarily resigned from her high-paying corporate job immediately
after the separation. She subsequently filed a petition under Section 125
of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) and Section 24 of the Hindu
Marriage Act (HMA), claiming she was unable to maintain herself and
demanded a monthly maintenance of ₹1.5 Lakhs from Rahul, who earns ₹3
Lakhs per month. Rahul contested the petition, presenting her pristine
educational credentials and employment history, arguing she was willfully
remaining unemployed solely to extort him.
cases.issues:
Is a highly educated, professionally qualified wife who voluntarily
abandons her lucrative career entitled to claim maintenance under Section
125 CrPC or Section 24 HMA?

What is the jurisprudential distinction between "actual earning" and
"earning capacity" when determining the inability to maintain oneself?

Does the law permit a spouse to weaponize maintenance statutes by
intentionally remaining idle to place a financial burden on the estranged
partner?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Neha)
Neha argued a strict, literal interpretation of Section 125 CrPC. The
statute provides for a wife who is "unable to maintain herself." She
argued that at the present moment, she has zero income and no savings,
rendering her factually unable to survive without his support. She
contended that the breakdown of the marriage caused her severe mental
trauma, making it impossible for her to continue in a high-stress
corporate environment. She argued that the court must look at her current
financial reality, not her theoretical capability.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Rahul)
Rahul relied on modern family law jurisprudence, citing cases like
Bhagwan v. Kamla Devi and rulings from various High Courts asserting that
Section 125 is meant to prevent vagrancy and destitution, not to fund
parasitic vengeance. He argued that Neha is not a destitute woman; she is
a highly qualified professional who made a calculated, malicious decision
to quit her job solely to invoke the maintenance statutes. He argued that
"unable to maintain" implies an inherent, inescapable inability (due to
illness, age, or lack of education), not a voluntary refusal to work.
cases.judgment:
The Family Court ruled in favor of Rahul. Neha's petition for permanent
maintenance under Section 125 CrPC was dismissed. The Defendant
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a pragmatic judgment reflecting the realities of
modern, egalitarian marriages. The judge explicitly rejected the archaic
notion that a husband is an absolute financial guarantor regardless of
the wife's capabilities. The Court analyzed the legislative intent of
Section 125, which is to provide social justice and prevent vagrancy, not
to create an avenue for unearned enrichment.

The Court drew a sharp line between "actual earning" and "earning
capacity." A wife who is genuinely unable to find work despite her
qualifications is entitled to support. However, Neha had a proven,
unbroken track record of high-income employment and resigned without any
documented medical necessity immediately upon separation. The Court ruled
that voluntary idleness by a highly qualified professional constitutes a
deliberate suppression of earning capacity. The law will not permit a
spouse to weaponize their own unemployment to extract punitive
maintenance from the other. Because she possessed the absolute capacity
to maintain herself at a high standard of living, she failed the
foundational test of the statute.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case redefines the parameters of Maintenance (Section 125 CrPC /
Section 24 HMA) in the context of Qualified Spouses. It establishes the
legal principle that voluntary idleness or deliberate resignation by a
highly educated, employable spouse completely negates their claim of
being "unable to maintain themselves," barring them from claiming
maintenance purely as a punitive measure.

cases.title: State Bank of India v. Kapoor Industries
cases.facts:
Kapoor Industries, a publicly traded mining conglomerate, discovered a
massive, highly lucrative bauxite deposit in a remote, ecologically
fragile tribal region. The extraction would generate ₹5,000 Crores in
profit over five years, heavily boosting shareholder dividends. However,
the environmental impact assessment revealed that the mining operations
would permanently pollute the local water table, displacing thousands of
indigenous families and destroying their agricultural livelihood.

The Board of Directors, facing immense pressure from major institutional
investors (including the State Bank of India, which held a 15% equity
stake), voted 7-to-2 to proceed with the mining project to maximize
shareholder value. Two dissenting independent directors filed a petition
before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) seeking an injunction
against the project. They alleged the Board was breaching its fiduciary
duties under Section 166(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, which mandates
directors to act in the best interests of the community and the
environment.
cases.issues:
Under Section 166(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, does a director's
fiduciary duty to protect the environment and community legally override
their traditional duty to maximize profits for shareholders?

Can a corporate board be held legally liable for "Oppression and
Mismanagement" if they approve a highly profitable project that causes
severe ecological and social devastation?

How does the NCLT balance the doctrine of Shareholder Primacy against
modern statutory Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and stakeholder
theory?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Dissenting Directors)
The Dissenting Directors anchored their case in the progressive overhaul
of Indian corporate law. They argued that Section 166(2) completely
abolished the archaic Anglo-American doctrine of absolute "Shareholder
Primacy." The statute legally elevates the "community" and the
"environment" to the status of primary stakeholders. By voting to execute
a project that guarantees the destruction of indigenous livelihoods and
water sources, the majority directors explicitly violated their statutory
fiduciary duty to the environment. The plaintiffs argued this willful
ecological blindness constitutes corporate mismanagement, justifying an
NCLT injunction to halt the mining.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Majority Board & SBI)
The Majority Board and SBI argued that a corporation is an economic
engine, not a charity. They contended that Section 166(2) is directory
and aspirational, not a veto over commercial viability. The company had
obtained the basic environmental clearances from the state (albeit
controversial ones) and pledged the statutory 2% CSR funds to build a
hospital for the displaced tribals. They argued that abandoning a ₹5,000
Crore asset would breach their paramount fiduciary duty to the
shareholders (who invested for returns, not environmental activism). They
warned that allowing independent directors to halt profitable operations
via the NCLT would paralyze corporate decision-making in India.
cases.judgment:
The NCLT ruled in favor of the Dissenting Directors. The Tribunal granted
an injunction halting the mining project and ordered the Board to
commission an independent, binding ecological audit before any further
action. The Plaintiffs prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Tribunal delivered a groundbreaking interpretation of modern
corporate governance. The judge decisively ruled that the 2013 Companies
Act permanently shifted India from a "Shareholder Primacy" model to an
"Enlightened Shareholder Value" (Stakeholder) model. Section 166(2) is
not mere boilerplate; it imposes a hard, enforceable legal obligation on
directors to actively safeguard the environment.

The NCLT noted that generating profit is a core corporate function, but
it cannot be pursued through the absolute devastation of surrounding
communities. Allocating 2% of profits to CSR does not grant a company a
license to destroy an ecosystem with the remaining 98%. The Board's
decision to consciously ignore the devastating environmental impact
assessment in favor of short-term dividends constituted a gross breach of
their fiduciary duty to the environment. The Tribunal held that a project
that causes irreparable ecological harm is inherently hostile to the
long-term sustainability of the company itself, thereby constituting
actionable mismanagement.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a monumental precedent regarding Directors' Fiduciary
Duties (Section 166(2) of the Companies Act, 2013). It establishes the
absolute legal principle that the duty to protect the environment and the
community is legally enforceable and can override the mandate to maximize
short-term shareholder profit, allowing the NCLT to halt ecologically
destructive corporate actions.

cases.title: Sharma Holdings v. Verma Enterprises
cases.facts:
The Sharma family was embroiled in a bitter, decade-long civil suit
regarding the partition of a highly valuable commercial complex in
Mumbai. The property was jointly owned by two brothers, Anil and Sunil
Sharma. While the partition suit was actively pending in the Bombay High
Court (with no stay order explicitly forbidding the sale), Sunil Sharma
secretly executed a registered sale deed, transferring his 50% undivided
share of the complex to Verma Enterprises, a third-party commercial
developer, for ₹50 Crores.

Verma Enterprises conducted a standard title search, which showed Sunil's
name on the deed, but they failed to check the active litigation
registry. Two years later, the High Court finally decreed the partition
suit, awarding the entire commercial complex to Anil Sharma, while
compensating Sunil with other family properties. Anil demanded Verma
Enterprises vacate the complex. Verma Enterprises refused, arguing they
were a Bona Fide Purchaser for Value Without Notice and their registered
sale deed was protected. Anil filed an eviction suit invoking Section 52
of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (Doctrine of Lis Pendens).
cases.issues:
Does the Doctrine of Lis Pendens (Section 52 TPA) absolutely void the
sale of immovable property executed while a suit regarding rights to that
property is pending?

Can a third-party buyer successfully invoke the equitable defense of
being a "Bona Fide Purchaser for Value Without Notice" to defeat the
doctrine of Lis Pendens?

Does the absence of a specific judicial stay order or injunction during
the trial permit a party to alienate the disputed property?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Anil Sharma)
Anil Sharma relied strictly on the absolute statutory mandate of Section
52 of the Transfer of Property Act. He argued that Lis Pendens translates
to "pending litigation." The law unequivocally dictates that during the
active pendency of any suit in which a right to immovable property is
directly in question, the property cannot be transferred by any party to
the suit so as to affect the rights of any other party under any decree
which may be made. He argued that Verma Enterprises' ignorance of the
suit is legally irrelevant. The sale is strictly subservient to the final
decree. Since the decree awarded the whole property to Anil, Verma's
purchase deed is legally worthless.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Verma Enterprises)
Verma Enterprises argued on principles of equity and commercial
certainty. They asserted they paid ₹50 Crores in absolute good faith
after reviewing valid municipal title documents. They argued that holding
innocent third-party purchasers liable for undisclosed, decades-long
family litigation destroys the sanctity of registered property
transactions. They pointed out that Anil never bothered to secure a
temporary injunction or a stay order on the sale from the court during
the 10-year trial. In the absence of an injunction, they argued, Sunil
was legally free to alienate his share, and their bona fide status should
protect their investment.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court ruled entirely in favor of Anil Sharma. The Court
declared the sale deed executed to Verma Enterprises invalid and ordered
their immediate eviction from the commercial complex. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a rigid enforcement of statutory property law. The
judge ruled that the Doctrine of Lis Pendens (Section 52) is not based on
the equitable doctrine of "notice," but on the absolute necessity of
judicial supremacy. If parties were allowed to sell disputed properties
during a trial, litigation would become endless, as every new buyer would
have to be impleaded, making it impossible for a court to ever execute a
final decree.

The Court firmly rejected the "Bona Fide Purchaser" defense. Under
Section 52, it is legally immaterial whether the buyer knew about the
lawsuit or not. A purchaser who buys property subject to active
litigation steps into the shoes of the seller and is absolutely bound by
the final outcome of that litigation. Furthermore, the Court clarified
that an explicit stay order or injunction is not required for Lis Pendens
to operate; the mere active pendency of the suit automatically freezes
the legal capacity of the parties to independently transfer title. Verma
Enterprises assumed a fatal commercial risk by failing to conduct a
thorough litigation search.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly enforces the Doctrine of Lis Pendens (Section 52 of
the Transfer of Property Act, 1882). It establishes the absolute legal
principle that property alienated during active litigation is strictly
subject to the final decree of the court, and the equitable defense of a
"Bona Fide Purchaser for Value Without Notice" is entirely invalid and
inapplicable in such scenarios.

cases.title: Arun Kumar v. Central Adoption Resource Authority
cases.facts:
Arun Kumar, a 35-year-old unmarried, financially secure, and highly
educated professional, applied to the Central Adoption Resource Authority
(CARA) to adopt a child. In his application, he explicitly stated his
preference to adopt a female child, citing a deep personal desire to
provide a nurturing home to a girl in a society where female orphans are
often marginalized.

CARA summarily rejected his application based on Regulation 5(2)(a) of
the Adoption Regulations, 2022, which explicitly states: "A single male
shall not be eligible to adopt a girl child." Arun filed a writ petition
in the Supreme Court of India, challenging the constitutional validity of
this specific regulation. He argued that it is a draconian, archaic rule
that violates his fundamental rights to equality (Article 14) and the
right to form a family (Article 21), while enforcing blatant gender
discrimination.
cases.issues:
Does Regulation 5(2)(a) of the CARA Guidelines, barring a single male
from adopting a female child, violate the fundamental right to Equality
before the Law under Article 14 of the Constitution?

Does the prohibition violate a single man's Right to Life and Personal
Liberty (Article 21), which encompasses the right to parenthood and
family formation?

Is the regulation a valid, protective measure based on "intelligible
differentia" aimed at ensuring the safety and welfare of vulnerable
female children?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Arun Kumar)
Arun Kumar argued that the regulation is rooted in toxic, misandrist
stereotypes that presume all single men are inherent threats to female
children. He pointed out the blatant hypocrisy in the regulations: a
single female is legally permitted to adopt a child of any gender. This
creates an arbitrary gender binary that violates Article 14 (Equality)
and Article 15 (Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of sex). He
argued that parenthood is a fundamental facet of Article 21, and the
State cannot deny a fit, capable citizen the right to father a daughter
based purely on his biological sex. He urged the court to evaluate
prospective parents based on rigorous individual background checks, not
blanket discriminatory bans.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (CARA / Union of India)
CARA defended the regulation invoking the doctrine of Parens Patriae.
They argued that in matters of adoption, the fundamental rights of the
prospective parent are entirely secondary to the paramount welfare and
safety of the child. They argued that the regulation is based on an
"intelligible differentia" with a rational nexus to the objective of
child protection. Given the grim realities of child sexual abuse and
exploitation in India, CARA argued that placing a vulnerable female
orphan in the exclusive custody of a single male carries inherent,
statistically elevated societal risks. They argued that the State, acting
as the ultimate guardian, has the absolute right to impose prophylactic
restrictions to preemptively shield female orphans from potential harm.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the CARA
regulation. Arun Kumar's writ petition was dismissed. The Defendant
(Union of India) prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Supreme Court delivered a highly cautious and protective judgment.
The Court acknowledged the plaintiff's desire for parenthood but drew a
sharp distinction between biological reproduction and statutory adoption.
The judge ruled that adoption is not a fundamental constitutional right
of the adult; it is a statutory privilege created exclusively for the
benefit of the orphaned child.

Addressing the Article 14 challenge, the Court applied the test of
reasonable classification. The judge noted that the classification
between single men and single women regarding the adoption of female
children is not born of misandry, but of objective, tragic social
realities regarding the disproportionate vulnerability of female children
to abuse. The State has a compelling interest in minimizing risk vectors.
While acknowledging that men like Arun Kumar could be exceptional
fathers, the Court held that administrative bodies must create broad
prophylactic rules to protect the most vulnerable. The Court concluded
that prioritizing the absolute safety of the girl child provides a
rational nexus for the gender-based restriction, meaning it does not fail
the test of constitutional equality.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes a critical boundary in Adoption Law and Article 14
(Equality). It reinforces the legal principle that in adoption
proceedings, the paramount welfare and safety of the child overwhelmingly
supersede the prospective parent's right to family formation (Article
21). It affirms that the State can impose gender-based restrictions on
adoption (e.g., barring single men from adopting girls) as a valid,
protective classification to safeguard vulnerable orphans.

cases.title: Desai v. FastTransit Transport Ltd.
cases.facts:
Mrs. Desai, a 40-year-old mother, was standing on the balcony of her
third-floor apartment. She watched as her 10-year-old son crossed the
quiet residential street below. Suddenly, a massive delivery truck owned
by FastTransit Transport Ltd., driven by a heavily intoxicated driver at
80 km/h, careened into the street, jumped the curb, and brutally ran over
her son, killing him instantly.

Mrs. Desai witnessed the entire horrific event from the balcony. She did
not suffer any physical impact or threat of physical impact herself.
However, the sheer horror of watching her child mangled caused an
immediate, severe psychiatric collapse. She was diagnosed with profound
Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and severe clinical depression,
requiring institutionalization and rendering her permanently unable to
work. She sued FastTransit Ltd. under the law of torts, seeking massive
compensation for "Nervous Shock" and psychiatric injury caused by their
driver's gross negligence.
cases.issues:
Can a plaintiff recover damages in tort for pure psychiatric injury
(Nervous Shock) resulting from witnessing an accident, when they
themselves were in no physical danger?

What are the legal prerequisites ("Control Mechanisms") required to
establish a duty of care for psychiatric injury caused to secondary
victims (bystanders)?

Is the emotional devastation of a mother witnessing her child's death a
foreseeable consequence of reckless driving?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mrs. Desai)
Mrs. Desai relied on the evolution of tort law regarding psychiatric
harm, citing landmark English precedents like McLoughlin v. O'Brian and
Alcock v. Chief Constable of South Yorkshire Police, which have
persuasive value in India. She argued that the driver owed a duty of care
not just to pedestrians, but to foreseeable secondary victims. A mother
witnessing the violent death of her child is the most foreseeable
scenario of catastrophic emotional shock. She argued that medical science
recognizes severe PTSD as a tangible, debilitating physical illness of
the brain, not mere "grief" or "sorrow." Therefore, the negligence of the
driver was the direct, proximate cause of her permanent medical
disability, warranting full compensatory damages.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (FastTransit Ltd.)
FastTransit Ltd. conceded the driver's negligence regarding the death of
the boy but fiercely contested the claim for the mother's psychiatric
injury. They argued for the "Floodgates" theory. If courts begin awarding
massive damages to bystanders who simply watch an accident without being
in the "zone of physical danger" themselves, it would impose infinite,
crushing liability on transport companies. Every accident has witnesses.
They argued that while her grief is immense, it is an indirect, remote
consequence of the accident. The law of negligence should strictly
compensate only those who suffer direct physical impact or imminent fear
of physical impact.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mrs. Desai. FastTransit Ltd. was held
vicariously liable for the severe psychiatric injury caused to the mother
and ordered to pay substantial compensatory damages. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a modern, compassionate adaptation of tort law,
officially cementing the doctrine of "Nervous Shock" in Indian
jurisprudence. The judge completely discarded the archaic requirement
that a plaintiff must be in the "zone of physical danger" to claim
psychiatric damages.

The Court adopted the strict "Control Mechanisms" from the Alcock case to
prevent the opening of floodgates. To succeed as a secondary victim, a
plaintiff must prove three things: (1) a close tie of love and affection
to the primary victim (e.g., parent/child); (2) physical and temporal
proximity to the accident or its immediate aftermath (she saw it happen
in real-time); and (3) the psychiatric injury must be caused by a sudden,
shocking event, not a gradual realization.

Mrs. Desai perfectly fulfilled all three criteria. The Court ruled that
it is entirely and reasonably foreseeable that driving a truck recklessly
into a residential neighborhood will not only crush bodies but will
inflict catastrophic, recognizable psychiatric illnesses upon the close
relatives who witness the horror. Psychiatric trauma is a tangible
medical injury, and the tortfeasor is absolutely liable for it.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case formally establishes the Tort of Psychiatric Injury (Nervous
Shock) for Secondary Victims. It sets the legal principle that a
plaintiff who suffers no physical impact can still recover massive
damages for severe psychiatric illness if they witness a sudden,
horrifying accident involving a close relative, provided they meet the
strict criteria of relational, spatial, and temporal proximity.

cases.title: Sharma v. Sharma
cases.facts:
In 2018, Mr. R.K. Sharma, a wealthy businessman facing severe, ongoing
tax evasion investigations by the Income Tax Department, purchased a
highly lucrative commercial shopping complex in Gurugram. To hide this
massive asset from the authorities and avoid attachment, he purchased the
property entirely with his own illicit funds but registered the sale deed
exclusively in the name of his 25-year-old son, Aman Sharma. R.K. Sharma
kept all the original title documents in his personal safe and collected
all the commercial rent in cash.

In 2025, a bitter family dispute erupted. Aman, realizing the property
was legally registered in his name, forcibly evicted his father's rent
collectors, took physical control of the complex, and began negotiating a
sale to a third party. R.K. Sharma filed a civil suit seeking an
injunction against the sale and a declaration that he was the absolute,
real owner of the property, claiming Aman was merely a "Benamidar" (name-
lender) holding the property in a fiduciary capacity.
cases.issues:
Under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 (as amended in
2016), can a person who buys property in the name of another to defeat
creditors/taxes reclaim the property from the ostensible owner?

Does purchasing property in the name of a child automatically trigger the
statutory exception of "fiduciary capacity" or "benefit of the child,"
rendering the transaction legal?

Does the equitable doctrine of In Pari Delicto (in equal fault, the
position of the defendant is stronger) bar the father from seeking
judicial relief?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (R.K. Sharma - Father)
R.K. Sharma argued that he provided 100% of the consideration (money) for
the property. He retained the title deeds and enjoyed the usufructs
(rent), proving he never intended to "gift" the property to his son. He
relied on Section 2(9) of the amended Benami Act, which provides an
exception for property purchased in the name of a spouse or child,
provided the consideration is paid out of "known sources." He argued that
as a father, he bought it for the future benefit of his son, and
therefore, it is not an illegal Benami transaction, but a property held
in trust, allowing him to reclaim it when the son acts adversely.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Aman Sharma - Son)
Aman argued a lethal, statutory defense. He invoked Section 4 of the
Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, which strictly prohibits any suit
to enforce any right in respect of any property held benami against the
person in whose name the property is held. He further demolished his
father's reliance on the "child exception." The exception strictly
requires the money to come from known, legal sources. Aman presented
evidence that the money used was entirely illicit, unaccounted "black
money" used specifically to defraud the Income Tax Department. Therefore,
it was an illegal Benami transaction. Aman argued that the courts cannot
help a man recover property he hid specifically to commit a fraud against
the State.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court dismissed R.K. Sharma's suit. The Court refused to grant
the declaration of ownership or the injunction, effectively leaving the
property in the legal possession of the son, Aman Sharma. The Defendant
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a ruthless application of the Benami Prohibition Act,
completely stripping the father of his hidden asset. The judge ruled that
the primary legislative intent of the Act is to destroy the practice of
hiding black money in real estate. Section 4 imposes an absolute
statutory bar: the real owner cannot sue the benamidar to recover the
property.

The Court examined the father's attempt to use the "child exception." The
judge noted the crucial caveat: the money must be from known sources.
Because R.K. Sharma used illicit funds specifically to evade tax
authorities, the transaction was an illegal, mala fide Benami purchase,
not a legitimate family investment. Applying the maxim In Pari Delicto,
the Court ruled that when a plaintiff must rely on their own illegality
(tax evasion) to prove their case, equity will slam the door in their
face. The Court will not act as a recovery agent for a fraudster. While
the son's actions were morally treacherous, the strict application of the
statute leaves the legal title exactly where the father fraudulently
placed it.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly enforces the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act. It
establishes the absolute legal principle that a person who purchases
property in another's name using illicit funds to defeat creditors or
taxes is statutorily barred from recovering that property. The courts
will apply the doctrine of In Pari Delicto to deny any equitable relief
to the fraudulent purchaser.

cases.title: State of Rajasthan v. Vidyavati's Heirs
cases.facts:
A Rajasthan State Police Jeep, driven by Constable Ramesh, was returning
to the central police lines after dropping off a senior Superintendent of
Police at a high-level government administrative meeting. The jeep was
not responding to an emergency, nor was it pursuing a suspect. While
driving recklessly and at high speed, Constable Ramesh lost control of
the vehicle and ran over a pedestrian, Mr. Sen, who was walking on the
footpath. Mr. Sen suffered fatal injuries. His widow, Vidyavati, filed a
civil suit for damages under the Law of Torts, claiming vicarious
liability against the State of Rajasthan for the fatal negligence of its
employee acting in the course of his employment.
cases.issues:
Is the State vicariously liable for the tortious acts (negligence)
committed by its employees in the course of their employment?

Can the State claim absolute immunity under the archaic doctrine of
"Sovereign Immunity" for the actions of a police vehicle?

What is the legal distinction between a "Sovereign Function" and a "Non-
Sovereign Function" regarding state liability in modern tort law?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Vidyavati's Heirs)
The Plaintiff anchored her case in the landmark Supreme Court judgment
State of Rajasthan v. Vidyavati. She argued that the archaic British
maxim "The King can do no wrong" has no place in a modern democratic
republic governed by a Constitution. The State, like any massive
corporate employer, must be held vicariously liable for the negligence of
its servants. She argued that driving a jeep from a meeting back to a
garage is a routine transport activity, not an inherently "sovereign" act
that only the State can perform. Therefore, the State enjoys no special
immunity and must compensate the victim's family for the loss of life
caused by its driver.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (State of Rajasthan)
The State invoked the defense of Sovereign Immunity, tracing it back to
the East India Company. They argued that the police force is the ultimate
manifestation of sovereign power (maintenance of law, order, and state
security). They contended that the jeep and the driver were an integral
part of the police machinery. Holding the State financially liable for
accidents involving police vehicles would paralyze the executive
machinery and drain the public exchequer. They argued the plaintiff's
only remedy was to sue the driver personally for his individual
negligence, not the sovereign state.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court (and upheld by the High Court) ruled in favor of
Vidyavati's heirs. The State of Rajasthan was held vicariously liable for
the negligence of the police driver and ordered to pay substantial
compensatory damages to the widow. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a historic judgment dismantling the absolute shield
of sovereign immunity. The judge ruled that in a welfare state, the
government engages in countless activities that are identical to private
enterprise. The Court established a critical dichotomy: State functions
are divided into "Sovereign" (inalienable functions like declaring war,
administering justice, legislating) and "Non-Sovereign" (routine
administrative, commercial, or transport activities).

The Court analyzed the specific act that caused the harm. Constable
Ramesh was not driving to quell a riot, chase a terrorist, or execute a
warrant (which might arguably touch upon sovereign duties). He was simply
driving a car back to a garage. Driving a vehicle on a public road is a
routine activity that any private citizen or corporation performs.
Because the negligent act occurred during a non-sovereign function, the
State operates on the exact same legal footing as a private employer.
Under the doctrine of Respondeat Superior, the State is absolutely and
vicariously liable for the torts of its servant.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strikes a massive blow against archaic colonial law by severely
restricting Sovereign Immunity in Tort Law. It establishes the
fundamental legal principle that the State is strictly vicariously liable
for the negligence of its employees when engaged in "Non-Sovereign
Functions" (like routine transport), ensuring citizens have a financial
remedy against the government for administrative negligence.

cases.title: InnoTech Inc. v. MobileX Corp.
cases.facts:
InnoTech Inc., a global telecom research giant, holds several patents
essential to the operation of the 5G cellular network standard. Because
it is technologically impossible to build a 5G phone without infringing
these specific patents, they are designated as Standard Essential Patents
(SEPs). As a condition for their patents being adopted as the global 5G
standard, InnoTech signed a declaration with international standard-
setting organizations committing to license these SEPs on Fair,
Reasonable, and Non-Discriminatory (FRAND) terms.

MobileX Corp, an Indian smartphone manufacturer, began producing millions
of 5G devices. InnoTech approached MobileX, demanding a royalty of $5 per
device. MobileX refused, arguing that $5 was exorbitant, commercially
ruinous, and a blatant violation of the FRAND commitment, noting that
InnoTech charged larger Western companies only $1 per device. When
negotiations broke down, InnoTech filed a suit in the Delhi High Court
seeking a permanent injunction to completely halt the manufacturing and
sale of all MobileX 5G phones in India for patent infringement. MobileX
filed a counterclaim with the Competition Commission of India (CCI),
alleging abuse of dominant market position.
cases.issues:
Can a holder of a Standard Essential Patent (SEP) seek a devastating
permanent injunction against a willing licensee who disputes the royalty
rate?

Does demanding exorbitant and discriminatory royalty rates for an SEP
constitute a breach of the FRAND commitment and an Abuse of Dominant
Position under the Competition Act, 2002?

How must civil courts balance absolute patent rights against antitrust
laws in the high-tech telecom sector?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (InnoTech Inc.)
InnoTech argued traditional, absolute patent rights. They proved MobileX
was using their 5G technology without paying a single rupee. They argued
that a patent grants an absolute statutory monopoly, including the
absolute right to exclude others via an injunction. They contended that
"FRAND" is a flexible, negotiated commercial concept, not a rigid price
ceiling. Charging different rates based on global sales volume is
standard business practice, not discrimination. They argued that MobileX
was an "unwilling licensee" employing hold-out tactics to delay payment,
leaving an injunction as InnoTech's only remedy to stop the massive,
ongoing piracy of their intellectual property.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (MobileX Corp)
MobileX argued that SEPs fundamentally alter traditional patent law. By
convincing the world to adopt their technology as the mandatory 5G
standard, InnoTech secured an absolute monopoly. In exchange, they
surrendered their right to absolute exclusion by committing to FRAND.
MobileX argued that weaponizing the threat of an injunction (which would
bankrupt MobileX) to extort a $5 royalty rate-while charging competitors
$1-is textbook "Patent Hold-Up" and a gross Abuse of Dominant Position
under Section 4 of the Competition Act. They declared themselves a
willing licensee, ready to pay a court-determined fair rate, but argued
that granting an injunction would destroy Indian manufacturing.
cases.judgment:
The Delhi High Court refused to grant the permanent injunction to
InnoTech Inc., provided that MobileX deposited a court-determined interim
royalty rate (significantly lower than $5) into a secure escrow account
while the trial proceeded to determine the final FRAND rate. The
Defendant prevailed against the injunction.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a highly sophisticated judgment navigating the
collision of Intellectual Property and Antitrust Law. The judge ruled
that holding a Standard Essential Patent places the patentee in an
incredibly dominant, monopolistic position. The FRAND declaration is a
binding, enforceable legal commitment designed precisely to prevent the
patentee from holding the entire tech industry hostage.

The Court held that the traditional remedy of a permanent injunction is
exceptionally harsh in SEP cases. If a manufacturer is genuinely willing
to take a license and pay a fair rate, the SEP holder cannot use the
threat of an injunction as an extortion tactic to force acceptance of
discriminatory or exorbitant rates. Because MobileX demonstrated a
willingness to pay a judicially determined rate and deposited funds into
escrow, they were not an "unwilling licensee." The Court ruled that
granting an injunction would severely harm consumers by restricting
access to 5G technology and destroying competition. The dispute must be
resolved purely as a pricing dispute (determining the FRAND rate), not
via the nuclear option of a manufacturing ban.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a massive precedent at the intersection of IP and
Competition Law regarding Standard Essential Patents (SEPs). It
establishes the legal principle that SEP holders who commit to FRAND
terms generally cannot obtain permanent injunctions against "willing
licensees." Using the threat of an injunction to extort unreasonable
royalties constitutes Patent Hold-up, forcing courts to prioritize fair,
judicially determined compensation over the absolute right of exclusion.

cases.title: GreenZone Residents v. Voltaic Cell Corp.
cases.facts:
Voltaic Cell Corp. operates a massive lithium-ion battery manufacturing
facility located on the outskirts of an expanding urban center. On August
15, 2025, due to a microscopic, undetectable manufacturing defect in a
single thermal cooling pipe, a massive chemical fire broke out in the
storage warehouse. The fire released highly toxic hydrofluoric acid gas
into the atmosphere, which drifted into the adjacent GreenZone
residential colony. Hundreds of residents suffered severe respiratory
damage, requiring hospitalization.

GreenZone Residents filed a class-action tort suit seeking multi-crore
compensation. Voltaic Cell Corp. presented irrefutable evidence that they
had employed the highest global safety standards, passed all government
environmental inspections, and that the defect was a "latent defect"
completely unforeseeable despite rigorous quality control. They claimed
the defense of "inevitable accident" and argued they were not negligent.
cases.issues:
Does the archaic rule of Strict Liability (Rylands v. Fletcher), which
allows for exceptions like "Act of God" or "inevitable accident," apply
to modern hazardous industries in India?

Is Voltaic Cell Corp. absolutely liable for the damages caused by the
toxic gas escape, regardless of whether they exercised reasonable care?

What is the threshold for an industry to be classified as engaged in a
"hazardous or inherently dangerous" activity?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (GreenZone Residents)
The Plaintiffs relied entirely on the landmark Supreme Court judgment in
M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak case). They argued that
manufacturing volatile lithium-ion batteries using highly toxic chemicals
is an inherently dangerous activity. Therefore, the industry owes an
absolute and non-delegable duty to the community. They argued that the
English rule of Rylands v. Fletcher is obsolete in the Indian industrial
context. Once a hazardous substance escapes and causes harm, liability is
absolute. The absence of negligence, the presence of safety
certifications, or the unforeseeability of the latent defect are entirely
irrelevant defenses in the face of absolute liability.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Voltaic Cell Corp.)
The Defendant attempted to distinguish their operations from those in
M.C. Mehta. They argued that lithium batteries are an essential green
technology for national development, not a highly volatile chemical like
Oleum gas. They argued that imposing absolute liability without any proof
of fault or negligence would completely stifle technological innovation
and industrial growth in India. They maintained that because they acted
with the utmost care and the leak was a true, unavoidable accident, basic
principles of tort law dictate they should not be penalized.
cases.judgment:
The National Green Tribunal (NGT) and the High Court ruled overwhelmingly
in favor of the GreenZone Residents. Voltaic Cell Corp. was held
absolutely liable and ordered to pay exemplary compensation for medical
expenses and environmental remediation. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a robust reaffirmation of Indian environmental tort
jurisprudence. The judge explicitly ruled that the Rylands v. Fletcher
doctrine, with its myriad exceptions, is inadequate to protect citizens
in a modern industrialized economy. Adopting the M.C. Mehta principle,
the Court held that an enterprise engaged in a hazardous or inherently
dangerous industry for private profit assumes an absolute obligation to
ensure no harm results to anyone.

The Court classified the mass storage of toxic chemical components for
battery manufacturing as an inherently hazardous activity. The judge
reasoned that the economic necessity of the product (green energy) does
not grant the corporation immunity from the devastation its processes can
cause. If the enterprise is permitted to operate for profit, it must
absorb the cost of any resulting disasters as a strict operational
overhead. The defenses of "latent defect," "lack of negligence," and
"statutory compliance" were deemed utterly void.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly enforces the Doctrine of Absolute Liability. It
establishes the legal principle that enterprises engaged in hazardous or
inherently dangerous activities are strictly and absolutely liable for
any resulting harm. This liability is not subject to any of the
exceptions found in traditional Strict Liability, effectively cementing
No-Fault Liability for toxic industrial torts in India.

cases.title: CyberSync Pvt. Ltd. v. FinServe Bank
cases.facts:
FinServe Bank contracted CyberSync Pvt. Ltd., an IT firm, to develop a
bespoke, high-security core banking software system. The contract price
was ₹10 Crores. Clause 8 of the contract stipulated: "Time is of the
essence. In the event CyberSync fails to deliver the fully functional
software by December 31, 2024, CyberSync shall pay a penalty of ₹50 Lakhs
for every single week of delay."

Due to unexpected complexities in integrating legacy data, CyberSync
delivered the software four weeks late, on January 28, 2025. The software
was flawless upon delivery. FinServe Bank withheld ₹2 Crores (₹50 Lakhs x
4 weeks) from the final payment, citing Clause 8. CyberSync sued for the
recovery of the ₹2 Crores, arguing that FinServe Bank suffered zero
actual financial loss during January, as they were still beta-testing
other systems, and therefore the deduction was an illegal, exorbitant
penalty.
cases.issues:
Is a clause stipulating a massive, fixed weekly sum for delayed
performance enforceable as Liquidated Damages, or is it void as an in
terrorem Penalty?

Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, must the aggrieved
party (FinServe Bank) prove actual, quantifiable loss to claim the
stipulated amount?

Can a party enforce a severe delay clause if they suffered no actual
commercial detriment from the delay?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (CyberSync Pvt. Ltd.)
CyberSync argued that Indian contract law, unlike English law, strictly
prohibits punitive damages for breach of contract. Relying on Fateh Chand
v. Balkishan Das and Kailash Nath Associates v. DDA, they argued that
Section 74 dictates that only "reasonable compensation" can be awarded.
The ₹50 Lakhs per week clause was drafted purely as a threat to enforce
performance, not as a genuine, calculated pre-estimate of loss. Because
FinServe was unready to deploy the software in January regardless, they
suffered zero actual injury. Therefore, withholding ₹2 Crores constitutes
unjust enrichment.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (FinServe Bank)
FinServe Bank argued that both parties were highly sophisticated
commercial entities who entered into the agreement with full legal
counsel. They argued that in complex IT infrastructure projects,
quantifying exact financial loss caused by a delay is practically
impossible. Therefore, the pre-agreed sum should be recognized as a
genuine pre-estimate of liquidated damages. They asserted that courts
should not rewrite commercial contracts to rescue a defaulting party from
a bargain they willingly signed, and that "time is of the essence" makes
the delay a fundamental breach justifying the deduction.
cases.judgment:
The Commercial Court ruled in favor of CyberSync Pvt. Ltd. The Court
struck down the ₹2 Crore deduction as an illegal penalty, ordering
FinServe Bank to pay the withheld amount, allowing them to deduct only a
nominal sum for administrative inconvenience. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court provided a surgical analysis of Section 74 of the Contract Act.
The judge ruled that the nomenclature used by the parties ("penalty" or
"liquidated damages") is irrelevant; the court must examine the substance
of the clause. A sum is a penalty if it is extravagant and unconscionable
in comparison to the greatest loss that could conceivably be proved. The
Court found ₹50 Lakhs a week to be arbitrary and disproportionate.

Crucially, the Court clarified the evidentiary burden. While a party need
not prove exact mathematical loss if it's impossible to calculate, they
must prove that they suffered some legal injury or detriment. Since
FinServe Bank could not deploy the software anyway due to internal
delays, the late delivery caused them no operational or financial harm.
The Court held that Section 74 dispenses with proof of the extent of the
loss, but not the factum (existence) of the loss. Enforcing the deduction
would grant the bank a massive financial windfall for a victimless
breach, violating the compensatory ethos of Indian contract law.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case distinguishes between Liquidated Damages and Penalties (Section
74 of the Indian Contract Act). It establishes the legal principle that
extravagant delay clauses intended as a threat are void as penalties.
Courts will only award reasonable compensation, and the aggrieved party
must prove the existence of actual legal injury or loss to claim damages;
unjust enrichment from a victimless breach is barred.

cases.title: Sharma v. Verma Developers
cases.facts:
In January 2023, Mr. Sharma entered into a written, unregistered
"Agreement to Sell" with Verma Developers to purchase a flat for ₹1
Crore. Sharma paid ₹90 Lakhs upfront as consideration. In return, Verma
Developers handed over the physical keys and allowed Sharma to take
absolute possession of the flat. Sharma moved in, renovated the kitchen,
and began paying the property taxes. However, the formal Sale Deed was
never registered due to bureaucratic delays.

In 2025, property prices skyrocketed. Verma Developers, realizing they
could sell the flat for ₹2 Crores, secretly executed and registered a
formal Sale Deed transferring the exact same flat to a third party, Mr.
Gupta. Verma Developers then sent eviction notices to Sharma, claiming
that since Sharma only possessed an unregistered agreement, he had no
legal title under the Transfer of Property Act, and Mr. Gupta was the
absolute, lawful owner via the registered deed. Sharma filed a suit
invoking Section 53A (Part Performance) to protect his possession.
cases.issues:
Does an unregistered "Agreement to Sell" confer any legal protection
against eviction if the prospective buyer has already taken physical
possession of the property?

Can the equitable Doctrine of Part Performance (Section 53A of the
Transfer of Property Act) be used as a shield to defeat the legal title
of a subsequent registered purchaser?

What are the mandatory statutory prerequisites to invoke the protection
of Section 53A?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. Sharma)
Sharma argued that equity strictly protects his possession. Under Section
53A of the Transfer of Property Act (Doctrine of Part Performance), he
had fulfilled all statutory criteria: there was a written contract signed
by the transferor, he had paid almost the entire consideration, he had
taken physical possession in furtherance of the contract, and he was
willing to perform his remaining part (paying the final ₹10 Lakhs).
Therefore, the law debars Verma Developers (and anyone claiming under
them, like Mr. Gupta) from enforcing any right against his possession,
rendering the subsequent registered sale deed legally impotent to evict
him.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Verma Developers & Mr. Gupta)
The Defendants relied on a strict interpretation of the Registration Act,
1908, and Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act. They argued that
title to immovable property worth more than ₹100 can only pass via a
registered instrument. An unregistered agreement to sell does not create
any interest or charge on the property. Mr. Gupta argued he was a bona
fide purchaser with a legally registered title document, whereas Sharma
was essentially an unauthorized occupant relying on a legally deficient
piece of paper.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court ruled in favor of Mr. Sharma. The Court granted a
permanent injunction protecting Sharma's possession and declared that Mr.
Gupta's registered sale deed could not be used to evict him. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a classic application of equitable property law. The
judge affirmed that while it is true an unregistered agreement does not
confer legal title, Section 53A was explicitly drafted to prevent
transferors from exploiting this technicality to commit fraud. Section
53A is a statutory shield based on equity.

The Court verified that Sharma met all conditions: a written contract
existed, he took possession based on that contract, and he did some act
(renovations/tax payments) in furtherance of it. Once these conditions
are met, a statutory bar is raised. The transferor (Verma) is legally
barred from enforcing any rights against the transferee's possession.
Crucially, the Court ruled that this bar applies equally to anyone
claiming under the transferor-including the subsequent buyer, Mr. Gupta.
The Court noted that Mr. Gupta failed to exercise due diligence; had he
visited the flat, he would have seen Sharma living there, which
constitutes constructive notice of Sharma's equitable rights.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case firmly operationalizes the Doctrine of Part Performance
(Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882). It establishes the
legal principle that while an unregistered agreement does not transfer
title, it provides an absolute equitable shield to protect the possession
of a buyer who has fulfilled their contractual obligations, barring both
the original seller and subsequent registered purchasers from evicting
them.

cases.title: Vineeta's Heirs v. Rakesh HUF
cases.facts:
Mr. Rakesh, the patriarch (Karta) of a wealthy Hindu Undivided Family
(HUF) possessing extensive ancestral agricultural lands, died intestate
in 2001. He was survived by two sons and one daughter, Vineeta. Upon his
death in 2001, the two sons assumed control of the entire ancestral
estate, arguing that under the unamended Hindu Succession Act, 1956, only
male lineal descendants were coparceners (joint heirs).

In 2005, the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act was passed, granting
daughters equal coparcenary rights. In 2020, Vineeta filed a civil suit
demanding her 1/3rd equal share of the ancestral properties, seeking to
partition the estate. The brothers fiercely contested the suit. They
argued that the 2005 amendment was prospective, meaning it only applied
if the father (the Karta) was alive on September 9, 2005 (the date the
amendment came into force). Since their father died in 2001, the
succession had already opened and finalized under the old law, and
granting Vineeta a share now would unlawfully apply the amendment
retrospectively and destroy vested property rights.
cases.issues:
Under Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (as amended in 2005),
does a daughter have a right to claim an equal coparcenary share in
ancestral property if her father died prior to the enactment of the 2005
amendment?

Is the conferring of coparcenary rights on daughters under the 2005
amendment prospective, retrospective, or retroactive in nature?

Can an unpartitioned ancestral estate be subjected to a new claim of
coparcenary rights decades after the patriarch's death?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Vineeta's Heirs)
The Plaintiff anchored her case in the landmark 2020 Supreme Court
judgment Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma. She argued that the 2005
amendment fundamentally altered the nature of Hindu succession by
conferring coparcenary status on daughters "by birth," exactly like a
son. Because the right arises by birth, it is immaterial whether the
father was alive or dead on the date the amendment came into force (Sept
9, 2005). The plaintiff argued the amendment is retroactive-it operates
forward but is based on an event (her birth) that occurred in the past.
Since the HUF properties had never been legally, formally partitioned by
a court decree prior to 2004, the joint family property remained intact,
and she maintained an absolute right to demand her equal share.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (The Brothers)
The Defendants relied on older, conflicting Supreme Court judgments (like
Prakash v. Phulavati), which had held that the amendment required the
father and the daughter to both be living on the date of the amendment.
They argued that succession opens on the date of death. When the father
died in 2001, under the existing law, the property legally vested in the
sons. They argued that allowing a daughter to claim a share 20 years
later creates total chaos, unsettling countless property titles and
inheritance arrangements that were perfectly legal when they occurred.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court, bound by the recent Supreme Court Constitutional Bench
precedent, ruled unequivocally in favor of Vineeta. The Court ordered the
partition of the ancestral properties, granting Vineeta an equal 1/3rd
coparcenary share. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark application of gender equality in family
law. Following the Vineeta Sharma Constitutional Bench ruling, the judge
clarified the nature of the 2005 amendment. The Court ruled that
coparcenary rights are not inherited through succession upon death; they
are acquired absolutely by birth.

Because the right is inherent by birth, the requirement that the father
must be alive on the date of the 2005 amendment is legally absurd. The
statute substituted the daughter in the exact same position as a son. The
Court clarified that the amendment is "retroactive," meaning it confers a
right in the present based on an event (birth) from the past. The only
exception the law allows is if the ancestral property had been formally
and legally partitioned by a registered decree before December 20, 2004.
Since the brothers had simply been enjoying the property jointly without
a formal, registered partition, the estate remained an HUF, making it
fully subject to Vineeta's newly recognized, equal coparcenary claim.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case operationalizes the ultimate interpretation of Section 6 of the
Hindu Succession Act, 1956 (2005 Amendment). It establishes the absolute
legal principle that a daughter's right to ancestral coparcenary property
is acquired by birth, and it is entirely immaterial whether the father
was alive or dead on the date of the 2005 amendment, ensuring total
gender parity in Hindu property law.

cases.title: Apex Publishers v. Delhi University Copy Shop
cases.facts:
Three major international academic publishers (Apex Publishers) filed a
copyright infringement suit against a small photocopying shop located on
the campus of a prestigious central university in Delhi. The publishers
alleged that the shop, operating under a license from the university, was
mass-producing "course packs"-bound compilations of photocopied chapters
extracted from various highly expensive, copyrighted academic textbooks
published by Apex.

These course packs were sold to university students at a fraction of the
cost of the original books. Apex Publishers sought an immediate
injunction, arguing this was rampant, commercial-scale piracy that
destroyed their academic book market. The university and the copy shop
invoked Section 52(1)(i) of the Copyright Act, 1957, claiming the
reproduction of the materials was completely exempt from copyright
infringement as it fell under the doctrine of "Fair Dealing" for the
purpose of educational instruction.
cases.issues:
Does the mass photocopying of chapters from copyrighted books to create
student "course packs" constitute copyright infringement?

Does Section 52(1)(i) of the Copyright Act (reproduction by a teacher or
pupil in the course of instruction) encompass commercial photocopying
shops operating on university campuses?

How does the Court balance the strict property rights of international
publishers against the socio-economic reality of accessible education in
a developing nation?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Apex Publishers)
Apex Publishers argued for strict copyright enforcement. They asserted
that copying 50-100 pages of a textbook is not "fair dealing"; it is
wholesale reproduction that completely usurps the market for the original
book. They argued that Section 52(1)(i) was intended for a teacher
copying a single page on a blackboard or handing out a single worksheet,
not for a commercial vendor systematically reproducing hundreds of bound
volumes for profit. The publishers warned that permitting this
"institutionalized piracy" would destroy the economic incentive to
publish academic literature in India, ultimately harming the educational
ecosystem.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Copy Shop & University)
The University anchored its defense in the socio-economic mandate of the
Right to Education. They argued that academic books published abroad are
prohibitively expensive for Indian students. They invoked Section
52(1)(i) of the Copyright Act, which exempts the reproduction of any work
"by a teacher or a pupil in the course of instruction." They argued that
the copy shop is merely an agent of the university, acting as a
technological facilitator for the teacher's syllabus. A teacher assigning
reading material and a student copying it to study is the very essence of
"the course of instruction." They argued that copyright is not a divine
right of property, but a statutory right designed to balance public
access with creator compensation.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of the University and the Copy Shop. The
Court dismissed the publishers' suit and refused to grant an injunction,
declaring the creation and distribution of the course packs legal under
the educational exceptions of the Copyright Act. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a watershed judgment prioritizing educational access
over copyright monopolies, heavily mirroring the landmark Delhi
University Photocopy Case. The judge extensively analyzed Section
52(1)(i) of the Copyright Act. The Court ruled that copyright is not a
natural or common law right in India; it is strictly a statutory
creation, and its boundaries are defined by the legislature.

The judge noted that the legislature deliberately did not place a
quantitative limit (like "fair use" percentages in US law) on the amount
of material that can be copied "in the course of instruction." Education
is a continuous process. If a teacher determines that reading specific
chapters is necessary for the syllabus, the reproduction of those
chapters by the students-or by an agent (the copy shop) acting on their
behalf-falls squarely within the exemption. The Court held that the
socio-economic reality of India demands that knowledge cannot be locked
behind exorbitant paywalls. The reproduction was for instruction, not
commercial competition, and thus constituted valid fair dealing.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case establishes a monumental precedent regarding the Educational
Exception to Copyright (Section 52(1)(i) of the Copyright Act, 1957). It
establishes the legal principle that the mass reproduction of copyrighted
academic materials (course packs) for the specific purpose of university
instruction by students and teachers does not constitute copyright
infringement, elevating the societal right to education over absolute
intellectual property monopolies.

cases.title: Tax Commissioner v. Horizon Shell Holdings
cases.facts:
Horizon Holdings, a massive multinational telecom conglomerate, sought to
sell its highly lucrative Indian subsidiary to a rival company, yielding
a capital gain of ₹10,000 Crores. Under standard Indian tax law, this
transaction would incur a massive capital gains tax. To avoid this,
Horizon Holdings orchestrated a complex international corporate
restructuring. They created a cascading series of holding companies in
the Cayman Islands and Mauritius (tax havens). Instead of selling the
Indian subsidiary directly, Horizon Holdings sold the single share of a
Cayman Islands shell company (which technically owned the Mauritius
company, which owned the Indian company) to the rival buyer.

Because the transaction occurred between two foreign entities in a tax
haven regarding a foreign share, Horizon Holdings claimed the transaction
fell entirely outside Indian tax jurisdiction. The Indian Tax
Commissioner issued a show-cause notice demanding ₹3,000 Crores in
capital gains tax, arguing the entire corporate restructuring was a
fraudulent "colorable device" designed exclusively to evade Indian taxes
by masking the true nature of the transaction (the sale of Indian
assets).
cases.issues:
Can tax authorities pierce the corporate veil and ignore the separate
