legal entity status of offshore shell companies if their sole purpose is
tax avoidance?

What is the jurisprudential distinction between legitimate "Tax Planning"
and illegal "Tax Evasion" via corporate restructuring?

Does the sale of a share in a foreign holding company attract Indian
capital gains tax if the underlying asset driving the value of that share
is situated entirely in India?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Tax Commissioner)
The Tax Commissioner relied heavily on the "Substance over Form" doctrine
established in McDowell & Co. v. CTO. The State argued that courts must
look at the economic reality of the transaction, not the intricate
corporate illusions created by high-priced lawyers. The Cayman and
Mauritius entities had no offices, no employees, and zero independent
business purpose; they were pure shell companies. The entire ₹10,000
Crore value of the transaction was derived exclusively from the telecom
assets located on Indian soil. The State argued that creating a
circuitous routing of shares specifically to escape Indian tax
jurisdiction is a fraudulent, colorable device, and the corporate veil
must be pierced to tax the true economic transfer.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Horizon Shell Holdings)
Horizon Holdings relied on the bedrock principle of corporate law
(Salomon v. Salomon) and the landmark Vodafone International Holdings v.
Union of India judgment. They argued that foreign direct investment
relies on corporate structuring certainty. Tax planning-organizing one's
affairs to minimize tax liability within the framework of the law-is
completely legal. They argued that Indian tax law at the time did not
have a "look-through" provision for indirect transfers. A share of a
Cayman company is a Cayman asset. Selling it is a foreign transaction.
They argued the Tax Department cannot rewrite the law retrospectively or
penalize a company for utilizing legal international corporate structures
just because the state missed out on revenue.
cases.judgment:
The Supreme Court ruled in favor of Horizon Shell Holdings (mirroring the
Vodafone precedent context). The Court quashed the tax demand, ruling
that the transaction was a legitimate transfer of foreign shares and
outside Indian tax jurisdiction. The Defendant prevailed. (Note: This
prompted subsequent retroactive legislative amendments).
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment prioritizing legal certainty in
international corporate law. The judge ruled that while the State can
strike down obvious frauds, courts cannot presume that every complex
international corporate structure is a "colorable device." The Court
affirmed the distinction between tax evasion (illegal) and tax planning
(legal). Creating holding companies in tax-friendly jurisdictions is
standard global commercial practice.

The Court held that the corporate veil can only be pierced if the
subsidiary is a complete sham with no commercial substance. Because the
holding structures had been in place for years prior to the sale and
facilitated genuine foreign direct investment, they were valid legal
entities. Crucially, the Court ruled on the strict interpretation of tax
statutes. Since the Indian Income Tax Act (at that specific time) did not
explicitly contain provisions to tax "indirect transfers" of underlying
Indian assets, the executive could not artificially expand its
jurisdiction through judicial interpretation to tax the sale of a foreign
share between two foreign entities.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case highlights the strict boundaries of Piercing the Corporate Veil
in Taxation and the legality of Tax Planning. It establishes the
principle that in the absence of specific statutory provisions (like
anti-avoidance rules), courts will respect the separate legal personality
of offshore holding companies, and legitimate tax planning through
corporate restructuring cannot be penalized as tax evasion based purely
on "substance over form" arguments.

cases.title: EcoGuard NGO v. MegaMining Ltd.
cases.facts:
EcoGuard, a prominent environmental NGO, published a detailed, 50-page
investigative report on their website. The report alleged that MegaMining
Ltd., a multi-billion dollar extraction conglomerate, was systematically
violating environmental regulations in central India, illegally expanding
their mining footprint into protected tiger reserves, and bribing local
forest officials to falsify compliance audits. The report gained massive
traction, leading to public protests and a sharp drop in MegaMining's
stock price.

In retaliation, MegaMining Ltd. filed a staggering ₹10,000 Crore civil
defamation suit against the NGO and its five founding activists. The
corporation also sought a blanket pre-publication injunction (a gag
order) to force the NGO to immediately take down the report and prevent
them from publishing any further statements about the company. EcoGuard
argued the lawsuit was a classic SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public
Participation), designed not to win, but to bankrupt and silence critics
through the crushing cost of litigation.
cases.issues:
Can a massive corporate entity use exorbitant civil defamation suits
(SLAPP suits) to silence environmental critics and investigative NGOs?

Does a detailed investigative report published by an NGO fall under the
defense of "Fair Comment" and "Public Interest" in defamation law?

Under what circumstances will a civil court grant a pre-publication gag
order (prior restraint) against journalistic or activist publications?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (MegaMining Ltd.)
MegaMining Ltd. argued that a corporation has a legal reputation that is
fiercely protected under tort law. They asserted that the NGO's report
was riddled with unverified allegations and manipulated data,
specifically designed to cause them maximum financial harm and extort a
settlement. They argued that freedom of speech (Article 19(1)(a)) is
subject to reasonable restrictions, including defamation. By publishing
the report to millions globally via the internet without giving the
company a right of reply, the NGO acted with malicious intent. The
company demanded the ₹10,000 Crore damages to cover the immense drop in
market capitalization directly caused by the libelous report.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (EcoGuard NGO)
EcoGuard invoked the defense of Truth, Fair Comment, and Overriding
Public Interest. They presented satellite imagery and testimonies from
whistleblowers corroborating their report. More importantly, they argued
that the ₹10,000 Crore lawsuit was a SLAPP suit-an abuse of the judicial
process. The damages claimed were astronomically disproportionate to
reality, specifically engineered to terrorize and financially ruin a non-
profit organization. They fiercely opposed the gag order, relying on the
rule against "prior restraint." Gagging an NGO from speaking about
corporate environmental crimes violates the core democratic function of
free speech and allows powerful entities to operate in total darkness.
cases.judgment:
The High Court dismissed MegaMining's application for a gag order and
severely reprimanded the corporation. While allowing the trial for
defamation to proceed, the Court struck down the ₹10,000 Crore damages
claim as malicious and vexatious, directing MegaMining to amend the suit
to a realistic sum. The Defendant (EcoGuard) largely prevailed on the
equitable remedies.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a powerful defense of democratic speech and public
participation against corporate intimidation. The judge recognized the
lawsuit for exactly what it was: a SLAPP suit designed to freeze free
speech through financial terror. The Court noted that asking for ₹10,000
Crores from a non-profit is an inherently malicious abuse of the legal
process intended to intimidate, not to seek genuine legal redress.

Addressing the gag order (prior restraint), the Court relied on the
Bonnard v. Perryman principle. In defamation cases, injunctions against
publication are exceptionally rare and generally refused if the defendant
intends to plead the defense of "Truth" or "Justification" at trial.
Because EcoGuard produced prima facie evidence supporting their claims
(satellite data), the Court ruled it would be a gross violation of
Article 19(1)(a) to silence them pending a lengthy trial. The public has
an absolute right to know about alleged environmental crimes committed by
massive corporations, and the courts will not act as a private censorship
arm for billionaires.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case introduces crucial judicial pushback against SLAPP Suits
(Strategic Lawsuits Against Public Participation) in India. It reinforces
the legal principle against Prior Restraint (Pre-publication injunctions)
in defamation, establishing that courts will protect Freedom of Speech
(Article 19(1)(a)) and the defense of Fair Comment in matters of profound
public interest, refusing to gag critics if they have a prima facie
defense of truth.

cases.title: Dream11 Fantasy v. State of Karnataka
cases.facts:
Dream11 Fantasy operates a massive online platform where users pay an
entry fee to create virtual sports teams based on real-life cricket
players. Users earn points based on the actual statistical performance of
those players in live matches. The users with the highest points win a
pooled cash prize.

The State Government of Karnataka, aiming to curb online gambling
addiction, passed sweeping legislation banning all forms of online gaming
involving monetary stakes. The State Police initiated criminal
proceedings against Dream11's executives and shut down their operations
in the state, classifying the platform as an illegal gambling operation.
Furthermore, several users sued the platform for the return of their
entry fees, claiming the contracts they signed with Dream11 were
"Wagering Agreements" and therefore void ab initio under Section 30 of
the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
cases.issues:
Is participating in a daily fantasy sports platform a "Game of Chance"
(Gambling/Wagering) or a "Game of Skill"?

Does an online format involving monetary entry fees and cash prizes
automatically render the user contracts void as "Wagering Agreements"
under Section 30 of the Indian Contract Act?

Does a State Government have the legislative competence to ban platforms
that are fundamentally based on skill under the guise of gambling
regulations?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State of Karnataka & Users)
The State argued a strict, paternalistic interpretation of gambling laws.
They argued that regardless of the mechanics, any platform where millions
of users put in money hoping to win a larger payout is functionally
identical to a lottery or a casino. They asserted that while some
knowledge of cricket is needed, the ultimate outcome depends on highly
unpredictable real-world events (a player getting injured, sudden rain,
pitch conditions), making chance the predominant factor. Therefore, the
contracts between users and the platform are pure "Wagering Agreements."
Under Section 30 of the Contract Act, agreements by way of wager are
void, meaning the company is operating an illegal enterprise and all
contracts are legally nullified.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Dream11 Fantasy)
Dream11 anchored its defense in Supreme Court precedents (like the K.R.
Lakshmanan v. State of Tamil Nadu horse racing case) and specific High
Court rulings validating fantasy sports. They argued that their platform
passes the "Predominance of Skill Test." Success requires extensive
knowledge of the sport, player statistics, pitch conditions, and
strategic resource allocation (salary caps). It is fundamentally
different from betting on the outcome of a coin toss or a roulette wheel.
Because skill predominates over chance, it is a legitimate business
activity protected under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution (Freedom of
Trade and Profession). Consequently, the user contracts are valid,
enforceable commercial agreements, not void wagers under Section 30.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Dream11 Fantasy. The Court struck down
the relevant provisions of the state legislation that banned games of
skill and declared that fantasy sports do not constitute gambling or
wagering agreements. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a definitive technological update to the century-old
law of wagering. The judge meticulously dissected Section 30 of the
Contract Act. A wager requires two parties holding opposite views
touching the issue of a future uncertain event, where one wins and the
other loses. However, the law distinguishes between games of pure chance
and games of skill.

Applying the "Predominance of Skill Test," the Court evaluated the
mechanics of fantasy sports. The judge ruled that drafting a winning
virtual team requires significant dedication, statistical analysis, and
strategic foresight. The success of the user is not determined by the
roll of a dice, but by their superior knowledge of the sport compared to
other users. Therefore, skill is the predominant factor. The Court held
that games of skill, even when played for financial stakes, do not fall
under the legal definition of "gambling." Consequently, the contracts
between the users and the platform are legally valid, enforceable service
contracts, entirely exempt from the voidability provisions of Section 30
of the Indian Contract Act.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case clearly establishes the boundary of Wagering Agreements
(Section 30, Indian Contract Act) in the digital age. It cements the
Predominance of Skill Test, ruling that commercial platforms offering
games where skill dominates chance are valid businesses, and the user
contracts are legally enforceable, protecting them from blanket state
bans on gambling.

cases.title: Iyer v. D'Souza
cases.facts:
Mr. Iyer owned a small, single-story heritage bungalow in a densely
packed neighborhood in Chennai. For 22 years, his study room received
natural sunlight and ventilation through a large, west-facing window that
looked directly out over his neighbor's (Mr. D'Souza's) vacant, empty
plot of land.

In 2024, D'Souza decided to develop his vacant plot. He hired contractors
and rapidly erected a massive, three-story concrete wall exactly six
inches away from Iyer's study window, completely blocking out all natural
light and air, rendering the room pitch black and stuffy. Iyer
immediately filed a civil suit for a mandatory injunction to demolish the
wall, claiming he had acquired an absolute "Easement by Prescription" for
light and air under Section 15 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882, having
enjoyed it peacefully and without interruption for over 20 years.
cases.issues:
Can a property owner acquire a legally enforceable easement right to
light and air simply by having a window overlooking a neighbor's vacant
plot for 20 years?

Under Section 15 of the Easements Act, does the right to light and air
become absolute, and can it restrict the neighbor's fundamental right to
build on their own land?

What constitutes an "actionable obstruction" of an easement of light and
air warranting a mandatory demolition injunction?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. Iyer)
Iyer argued a straightforward application of Section 15 of the Easements
Act. The statute explicitly states that where the access and use of light
or air to any building have been peaceably enjoyed as an easement,
without interruption, for twenty years, the right to such access becomes
absolute and indefeasible. He proved through municipal records and
photographs that the window had existed unaltered for 22 years. He argued
that D'Souza slept on his rights; he could have built a wall 10 years ago
to block the window but chose not to. Now that the 20-year prescriptive
period had matured, Iyer held a vested property right, and D'Souza's wall
was an illegal nuisance and obstruction requiring immediate demolition.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Mr. D'Souza)
D'Souza argued a defense of absolute property ownership (Cuius est
solum). He asserted that nobody can acquire a right that completely
paralyzes a neighbor's ability to develop their own prime real estate. He
argued that allowing Iyer's window to dictate what D'Souza can build on
his own property effectively constitutes an uncompensated taking of land.
Furthermore, D'Souza relied on nuances in tort law, arguing that blocking
a window is not an actionable nuisance unless it makes the plaintiff's
house substantially uninhabitable. He argued Iyer had other windows on
the east side of the house, so the loss of one window was an
inconvenience, not a complete deprivation of light warranting the
destruction of a newly built, expensive concrete structure.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court ruled in favor of Mr. Iyer. The Court granted a mandatory
injunction ordering D'Souza to demolish the portion of the concrete wall
that obstructed Iyer's window. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a strict enforcement of prescriptive property rights,
reaffirming that long-standing usage calcifies into legal reality. The
judge strictly applied Section 15 of the Indian Easements Act. The law is
clear: 20 years of continuous, peaceable, open enjoyment of light and air
through a specific aperture creates an absolute, indefeasible right. It
does not matter if the neighbor's land is highly valuable. D'Souza had 20
years to erect a screen or a wall to interrupt the prescriptive clock,
but he failed to do so.

Addressing the "substantial uninhabitability" defense, the Court
clarified that an easement right is attached to the specific window that
earned the prescription. The fact that the house has other windows is
legally irrelevant. Obstructing a window that has enjoyed a 20-year
prescriptive right constitutes a clear, actionable infringement of a
vested property right. Because monetary damages cannot adequately
compensate for the permanent loss of natural sunlight and air in a
specific room, the equitable remedy of a mandatory injunction compelling
the demolition of the offending wall is the only appropriate legal
remedy.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case rigorously enforces the Acquisition of Easements by
Prescription (Section 15, Indian Easements Act, 1882). It establishes the
absolute legal principle that 20 years of uninterrupted enjoyment of
light and air creates a vested, indefeasible property right. A neighbor
cannot subsequently build structures that obstruct this specific right,
and courts will issue Mandatory Injunctions for demolition to protect it.

cases.title: Starlight Productions v. Aryan
cases.facts:
Aryan, a rapidly rising, highly bankable film actor, signed a highly
lucrative, exclusive 3-year contract with Starlight Productions, a
massive film studio. The contract contained a strict "Negative Covenant":
Aryan agreed that during the 3-year term, he would not act, direct, or
provide any creative services for any competing film studio or production
house under any circumstances.

One year into the contract, Aryan received a massively lucrative, career-
defining offer from a rival studio, Galaxy Films, to star in an
international blockbuster franchise. Tempted by the global exposure and
massive payout, Aryan breached his contract with Starlight, openly
abandoning their ongoing film shoot, and publicly signed on to star in
the Galaxy Films movie.

Starlight Productions immediately rushed to the High Court. Acknowledging
that they cannot force an actor to act (Specific Performance of personal
service is barred), Starlight filed a suit seeking a strict Prohibitory
Injunction to enforce the Negative Covenant, demanding the Court legally
bar Aryan from acting for Galaxy Films or anyone else for the remaining
two years of his contract.
cases.issues:
Under Section 14 and Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, can a
civil court grant an injunction to enforce a negative covenant in a
contract for personal service?

Does enforcing a negative covenant that prevents an actor from working
anywhere else amount to an illegal restraint of trade or profession under
Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act?

Is the studio entitled to paralyze the actor's career, or are monetary
damages for breach of contract the only viable remedy?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Starlight Productions)
Starlight anchored its case in Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act,
which explicitly empowers a court to grant an injunction to perform a
negative agreement, even if the court cannot specifically enforce the
positive agreement (making him act). They relied on landmark cases like
Lumley v. Wagner and Percept D'Mark v. Zaheer Khan. Starlight argued they
invested millions into launching Aryan's career based entirely on his
exclusivity. Aryan's unique star power cannot be easily replaced, making
monetary damages inadequate. They argued the negative covenant was freely
negotiated and essential to protect their commercial investment, and
preventing him from acting for rivals does not violate Section 27
(Restraint of Trade) because the restriction applies only during the term
of the contract, not after it ends.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Aryan)
Aryan argued that the injunction sought is a thinly veiled attempt to
force specific performance of a personal service contract, which is
absolutely barred under Section 14(c) of the Specific Relief Act. You
cannot force a person to act, sing, or paint. Aryan further argued that
enforcing the negative covenant would leave him completely unemployed and
unable to earn a livelihood for two years, effectively starving him into
submission to return to Starlight. He argued this constitutes a harsh,
unconscionable restraint of his fundamental right to practice his
profession (Article 19(1)(g) and Section 27 of the Contract Act). He
argued Starlight should simply sue him for quantified breach of contract
damages.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Starlight Productions. The Court granted
a Prohibitory Injunction strictly enforcing the negative covenant,
legally barring Aryan from acting in any competing film or project for
the remainder of the 3-year contract term. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a classic analysis of equity in entertainment and
sports contracts. The judge navigated the tension between Section 14
(barring specific performance of personal service) and Section 42
(allowing injunctions for negative covenants). The Court ruled that while
it cannot physically drag Aryan onto Starlight's movie set and yell
"Action," it possesses the absolute statutory power to ensure he does not
violate his explicit promise to not work for competitors.

The Court heavily addressed the "Restraint of Trade" argument. Relying on
settled jurisprudence, the judge ruled that a negative covenant operating
during the active term of an employment or exclusive service contract is
NOT an illegal restraint of trade under Section 27. It is a standard,
enforceable commercial exclusivity clause. The Court reasoned that Aryan,
a highly paid professional, voluntarily traded his freedom to work
elsewhere in exchange for millions of rupees. Allowing stars to casually
break exclusivity contracts the moment a better offer appears would
destroy the commercial foundation of the entertainment industry. The
injunction ensures the sanctity of the contract is respected.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case operationalizes Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963,
regarding Negative Covenants in Personal Service Contracts. It
establishes the legal principle that while courts will not force a person
to perform personal services, they will grant prohibitory injunctions
enforcing exclusive negative covenants during the contract term, ruling
that such exclusivity clauses do not constitute an illegal restraint of
trade under Section 27 of the Contract Act.

cases.title: State of Maharashtra v. Apex Deliveries
cases.facts:
Apex Deliveries operates a massive food-delivery application, connecting
customers with local restaurants and "delivery partners." On October 15,
2025, an Apex delivery partner, Rahul, was rushing to deliver a high-
priority "30-minute guarantee" order. Driving his personal motorcycle
recklessly on the wrong side of a busy Mumbai road, Rahul collided head-
on with a pedestrian, Mrs. Iyer, causing her severe spinal injuries and
permanent paralysis. Mrs. Iyer filed a civil tort suit for ₹5 Crores
against both Rahul and the corporate entity, Apex Deliveries. Apex filed
for dismissal, arguing that Rahul was not an "employee" but an
"Independent Contractor," utilizing his own vehicle and choosing his own
login hours, thus entirely shielding the company from vicarious liability
under the doctrine of Respondeat Superior.
cases.issues:
Is a platform-based "gig worker" legally classified as an employee
(contract of service) or an independent contractor (contract for service)
for the purposes of tortious liability?

Does an algorithmic application exercise sufficient "control" over a
delivery partner to establish a master-servant relationship?

Can a gig-economy platform be held vicariously liable for the negligence
of its partners while they are executing platform-assigned tasks?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
Mrs. Iyer (Plaintiff) argued that traditional labor distinctions must
evolve. Relying on the "Integration Test" and the "Control Test," she
argued that while Rahul owned the bike, Apex Delivery controlled his
economic reality. The algorithm dictated the route, the payout, the time
limit (which incentivized the reckless driving), and held the power to
penalize or "terminate" him via low ratings. She argued that Apex reaps
massive financial benefits from this delivery network; therefore, public
policy dictates they must internalize the costs of the accidents their
high-speed operational model inevitably generates, making them
vicariously liable as a de facto employer.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
Apex Deliveries (Defendant) argued a strict, literal interpretation of
contract law. Their "Terms of Service," signed by Rahul, explicitly
stated he was an independent micro-entrepreneur. They argued they merely
provide a technological matchmaking service. They do not pay a fixed
salary, provide insurance, or enforce mandatory working hours. They
argued that holding a software intermediary vicariously liable for the
autonomous, illegal traffic violations of millions of independent
freelancers would completely destroy the economic viability of the
platform economy in India.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mrs. Iyer. The Court pierced the
"independent contractor" classification, holding Apex Deliveries
vicariously liable for the negligence of the delivery partner, and
ordered them to pay joint and several compensatory damages. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark judgment adapting tort law to the gig
economy. The judge looked past the boilerplate "Terms of Service" to the
operational reality of the business model. Applying a modernized "Control
Test," the Court found that Apex exercises pervasive, algorithmic control
over its workers. By promising a "30-minute guarantee" to the consumer,
the platform actively mandated the speed and urgency of the task.
Furthermore, the delivery partner is fully integrated into the core
business of Apex; without riders, the app has no product. The Court ruled
that companies cannot exert totalitarian algorithmic control over a
worker's performance while simultaneously outsourcing all legal liability
to them. Consequently, for the duration of the active delivery, a master-
servant relationship legally exists.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case significantly evolves the doctrine of Vicarious Liability
(Respondeat Superior). It establishes the legal principle that
algorithmic control and economic integration within the "Gig Economy"
satisfy the requirements of a master-servant relationship, stripping tech
platforms of the "Independent Contractor" defense when their workers
commit torts while executing platform-directed tasks.

cases.title: NovaCorp Pharma v. The Patent Controller of India (Intellectual Property - Patent Evergreening and Section 3(d))
cases.facts:
NovaCorp Pharma, a multinational biomedical giant, held a 20-year Indian
patent for "GastroHeal," a highly successful, albeit expensive, drug used
to treat chronic gastric ulcers. In 2024, exactly six months before the
original patent was set to expire (which would allow cheap generic
versions to flood the market), NovaCorp filed a new patent application
for "GastroHeal-Pro." The new application was simply the exact same base
chemical compound (the active pharmaceutical ingredient), but bonded with
an additional, inactive salt molecule (a new crystalline form) that
slightly improved the drug's shelf-life in humid climates. NovaCorp
sought a fresh 20-year monopoly. The Patent Controller of India rejected
the application. NovaCorp appealed to the High Court, arguing their new
formulation was a novel, non-obvious invention deserving protection.
cases.issues:
Does the discovery of a new form of a known substance, which merely
improves stability but not therapeutic efficacy, qualify as a patentable
invention under the Patents Act, 1970?

How does Section 3(d) of the Patents Act prevent the practice of
"Evergreening" by pharmaceutical monopolies?

What is the legal threshold for demonstrating "enhanced therapeutic
efficacy"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
NovaCorp (Appellant) argued that "GastroHeal-Pro" met all traditional
patentability criteria: novelty, inventive step, and industrial
applicability. They spent ₹50 Crores researching the specific salt bond
to increase shelf life, which is a massive commercial and logistical
benefit in a tropical country like India. They argued a strict reading of
Section 3(d) stifles incremental innovation. They asserted that improving
a drug's stability and bioavailability is a significant scientific
advancement that deserves intellectual property protection to encourage
continuous pharmaceutical R&D.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The Patent Controller (Respondent), backed by intervening health NGOs,
relied heavily on the landmark Supreme Court judgment in Novartis v.
Union of India. They argued that Section 3(d) was explicitly drafted by
the Indian legislature to stop "Evergreening"-the abusive practice of
making minor, superficial tweaks to an expiring drug to unfairly extend a
monopoly. Under Section 3(d), a new form of a known substance is strictly
unpatentable unless it results in a significant enhancement of its known
therapeutic efficacy. The State argued that increased shelf-life is a
logistical benefit, not a therapeutic one (it does not cure the ulcer
better or faster). Therefore, the derivative compound fails the strict
statutory test.
cases.judgment:
The High Court upheld the decision of the Patent Controller and dismissed
NovaCorp's appeal. The patent for the derivative drug was denied. The
Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a robust defense of India's stringent public health
patent standards. The judge rigorously applied Section 3(d) of the
Patents Act, affirming the Novartis precedent. The Court ruled that
Indian patent law distinguishes between a genuine "invention" and a mere
"discovery" of a new property of an existing substance. For a
pharmaceutical derivative to be patentable, it must prove a demonstrable,
significant enhancement in therapeutic efficacy-meaning it must actually
heal the patient more effectively or safely than the original patented
drug. The Court found that NovaCorp's addition of a salt molecule only
improved commercial storage (shelf-life), which, while economically
useful, offers no new therapeutic healing value to the human body. The
application was deemed a textbook, bad-faith attempt at evergreening to
maintain artificially high drug prices.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case rigidly enforces Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, 1970, and the
doctrine against Patent Evergreening. It establishes the absolute legal
principle that incremental pharmaceutical modifications (like new salts
or polymorphs) are unpatentable unless they demonstrate a significant
enhancement in actual therapeutic efficacy, prioritizing public access to
affordable generic medicines over extended corporate monopolies.

cases.title: Sharma v. Royal Bank of Commerce
cases.facts:
Mr. Sharma, desperate for capital to save his failing manufacturing
business, took a commercial loan of ₹5 Crores from the Royal Bank of
Commerce in 2015. To secure the loan, he executed a mortgage by
conditional sale of his prime commercial warehouse. The mortgage deed
contained a specific, highly restrictive clause: "If the mortgagor fails
to repay the principal and interest in full within exactly 10 years (by
2025), the mortgagor's right to redeem the property shall be permanently
extinguished, and absolute ownership of the warehouse shall automatically
vest in the Bank without further legal proceedings." In 2026, a year
after the deadline, Sharma arranged the funds and approached the bank to
pay the entire debt plus penalty interest to redeem his warehouse. The
Bank refused, invoking the 10-year forfeiture clause, claiming they were
now the absolute owners. Sharma filed a civil suit to enforce his right
of redemption.
cases.issues:
Is a contractual clause that automatically extinguishes a mortgagor's
right to redeem their property upon a timeline default legally
enforceable?

Does the equitable maxim "Once a mortgage, always a mortgage" override
explicit, signed commercial contracts between sophisticated parties?

What constitutes an illegal "Clog on the Equity of Redemption" under
Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
Sharma (Plaintiff) relied on Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act,
which grants the mortgagor a statutory right to redeem the mortgaged
property upon payment of the debt. He argued the equitable doctrine
against "clogs on redemption." Any contractual condition inserted into a
mortgage deed that prevents, impedes, or penalizes the mortgagor from
reclaiming their property upon paying the debt is fundamentally void. He
argued that the 10-year automatic forfeiture clause was an
unconscionable, predatory term designed to steal a property worth far
more than the loan amount, violating the very essence of a mortgage,
which is merely a security for a debt, not a conditional sale.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
The Royal Bank of Commerce (Defendant) argued for the sanctity of
commercial contracts. They asserted that Sharma was a sophisticated
businessman who willingly signed the agreement with full legal
comprehension of the deadline. They argued that striking down explicit
commercial terms disrupts financial certainty in the banking sector. The
Bank contended that since Sharma breached the fundamental term of the 10-
year repayment window, the mortgage legally converted into an absolute
sale as explicitly agreed upon by the parties, severing his equitable
rights.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court ruled in favor of Mr. Sharma. The Court struck down the
forfeiture clause as an illegal clog on the equity of redemption,
ordering the Bank to accept the full repayment and transfer the warehouse
title back to Sharma. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a classic application of equitable property law,
severely restricting predatory lending terms. The judge ruled that the
fundamental nature of a mortgage is that it is merely a security for the
repayment of a loan. Under Indian law, the maxim "Once a mortgage, always
a mortgage" is absolute. Any clause in the mortgage deed that seeks to
convert the mortgage into a permanent sale upon default, or puts an
absolute time limit on the right of redemption, is considered a "Clog on
the Equity of Redemption." The Court held that Section 60 of the Transfer
of Property Act is a statutory right that cannot be contracted away, even
by consenting, sophisticated adults. Because the Bank's sole legitimate
interest is the recovery of its money with interest, not the acquisition
of the debtor's real estate, the forfeiture clause was declared void ab
initio.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly enforces the Right of Redemption (Section 60, Transfer
of Property Act, 1882). It establishes the absolute equitable principle
against any Clog on the Equity of Redemption, ruling that any contractual
clause attempting to permanently extinguish a mortgagor's right to
reclaim their property upon repayment of the debt is fundamentally void,
regardless of the parties' mutual agreement.

cases.title: DataCore Tech v. Desai
cases.facts:
Vikram Desai was a senior data scientist at DataCore Tech, specializing
in highly sensitive, proprietary machine learning algorithms for high-
frequency stock trading. His employment contract contained a strict "Non-
Compete Clause": "Upon termination or resignation, the Employee shall not
work for any competing financial technology firm, nor start an
independent competing business, within the territory of India for a
period of two (2) years." In 2025, Desai resigned and immediately joined
'Quantum Finance,' a direct competitor, for a massive salary increase.
DataCore Tech filed a civil suit seeking a permanent injunction to
enforce the 2-year non-compete clause, arguing Desai possessed intimate
knowledge of their trade secrets which he would inevitably use to benefit
his new employer, causing DataCore irreparable commercial damage.
cases.issues:
Is a post-employment non-compete clause that restricts a former employee
from joining a rival company legally enforceable under Indian law?

Does enforcing such a clause constitute an illegal "Restraint of Trade"
under Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872?

How does the law balance a corporation's right to protect its proprietary
trade secrets against a citizen's fundamental right to earn a livelihood?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant
DataCore Tech (Plaintiff) argued that their restriction was entirely
reasonable and necessary. They did not seek to prevent Desai from working
in IT generally, only in the hyper-niche sector of high-frequency
algorithmic trading for a limited duration of two years. They argued that
Desai had access to source code and business strategies that constitute
highly sensitive trade secrets. Relying on global commercial norms, they
argued that without enforcing post-employment non-competes, tech
companies have no mechanism to prevent predatory poaching by rivals
seeking to steal intellectual property, which would ultimately destroy
corporate R&D investment.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent
Desai (Defendant) anchored his defense in an absolute reading of Section
27 of the Indian Contract Act, which states that every agreement by which
anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or
business of any kind, is to that extent void. Relying on landmark Supreme
Court judgments like Percept D'Mark v. Zaheer Khan, he argued that while
non-competes are valid during the term of employment, Indian law rigidly
strikes down any post-termination restriction on a person's right to
work. He argued that forcing him to sit idle for two years strips him of
his fundamental right to a livelihood (Article 19(1)(g)). If DataCore
feared IP theft, their remedy was to sue for breach of confidentiality,
not to legally paralyze his career.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Vikram Desai. The Court refused to grant
the injunction, striking down the 2-year post-employment non-compete
clause as void and unenforceable. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a judgment highly protective of employee mobility.
The judge explicitly ruled that Indian contract law diverges
significantly from Western jurisdictions regarding restrictive covenants.
Under Section 27 of the Contract Act, the prohibition against restraint
of trade is absolute and non-negotiable. The statute does not recognize a
"reasonableness" test for post-employment restrictions. Once an
employment contract is terminated, any clause that prevents the former
employee from joining a competitor or exercising their lawful profession
is inherently void against public policy.

The Court acknowledged DataCore's legitimate anxiety regarding trade
secrets. However, the judge reasoned that a company cannot use a blunt
non-compete instrument to achieve confidentiality. If Desai actually
steals code or leaks specific client lists, DataCore can sue him under
intellectual property and confidentiality laws. But the court will not
issue a blanket injunction that robs an individual of their right to
apply their inherent skills, knowledge, and experience in the open market
to earn a living.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case rigorously enforces Section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872
(Agreement in Restraint of Trade). It establishes the absolute legal
principle that post-employment non-compete clauses are fundamentally void
and unenforceable in India, regardless of their "reasonableness,"
protecting an individual's absolute right to professional mobility and
livelihood after a contract terminates.

cases.title: The Estate of Verma v. The State
cases.facts:
Mr. Verma, a billionaire industrialist, possessed massive tracts of prime
real estate. Deeply distrustful of his extravagant sons, Verma executed a
complex, registered deed of family settlement in 2020. The deed
transferred the absolute ownership of the real estate to his eldest son,
Anil. However, the deed contained a strict, terrifying condition: "Anil
and his descendants shall enjoy the income of this property forever, but
they are absolutely prohibited from ever selling, mortgaging, or
alienating this property to any person outside the Verma bloodline.
Should any heir attempt to sell the land, the property shall instantly
forfeit and vest in the State Orphanage Trust." In 2025, Anil, facing
bankruptcy, attempted to sell a portion of the land to a commercial
developer. The State Orphanage Trust filed a suit to claim the property,
invoking the forfeiture clause. Anil counter-sued, claiming the condition
restraining alienation was void.
cases.issues:
Can a property owner transfer absolute title to an heir while
simultaneously imposing a condition that completely destroys the heir's
right to alienate (sell/mortgage) the property?

Does a condition perpetually tying up property within a specific
bloodline violate the "Rule Against Perpetuity" and Section 10 of the
Transfer of Property Act, 1882?

If a restraining condition is found void, does the entire transfer fail,
or does the transferee take the property free of the restriction?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (State Orphanage Trust)
The Trust argued that Mr. Verma was the absolute owner of the property
and had the sovereign right to dispose of it subject to any conditions he
chose. They argued that a donor is the master of his gift. Anil accepted
the property fully aware of the condition attached to it. The Trust
argued that Anil cannot approbate and reprobate-he cannot take the
benefit of the multi-crore land while discarding the burden of the
condition he agreed to. By attempting to sell the land, Anil triggered
the valid forfeiture clause, meaning the title legally shifted to the
charity.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Anil Verma)
Anil anchored his case in Section 10 (Condition restraining alienation)
and Section 14 (Rule against perpetuity) of the Transfer of Property Act.
He argued that the law abhors property being tied up endlessly. Section
10 explicitly states that where property is transferred subject to a
condition absolutely restraining the transferee from parting with or
disposing of their interest, the condition is void. Anil argued that
ownership inherently includes the right of alienation. Because his father
transferred absolute title to him, the subsequent condition permanently
stripping him of the right to sell it is a legal paradox and statutorily
void.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court ruled in favor of Anil Verma. The Court declared the
condition restraining alienation absolutely void, and affirmed Anil's
right to sell the property. The claim of the State Orphanage Trust was
dismissed. The Defendant prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a fundamental lesson on the nature of property
ownership. The judge applied a strict reading of Section 10 of the
Transfer of Property Act. The Court reasoned that the right of alienation
(to sell, gift, or mortgage) is the very lifeblood of property ownership.
You cannot give someone a car but legally forbid them from ever driving
it. The law views property as an economic asset that must remain freely
circulating in the market.

The Court ruled that Mr. Verma attempted to create an absolute restraint
on alienation, perpetually freezing the land within his bloodline. This
directly violates public policy and Section 10. Crucially, the Court
clarified the legal consequence of a void condition: when a condition
subsequent is declared void for illegality, the condition is severed, but
the underlying transfer remains perfectly valid. Therefore, Anil takes
the property absolutely, free from the dead hand of his father, and the
forfeiture clause favoring the orphanage is rendered legally impotent.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly enforces the Rule against Restraints on Alienation
(Section 10, Transfer of Property Act, 1882). It establishes the absolute
legal principle that if a property is transferred absolutely, any
condition that permanently restrains the new owner from selling or
alienating the property is legally void. The transferee inherits the
property free of the restriction.

cases.title: Genesis IVF Clinic v. Mr. & Mrs. Kapoor
cases.facts:
Mr. and Mrs. Kapoor, struggling with infertility for a decade, paid ₹15
Lakhs to Genesis IVF Clinic, a premier fertility center, for In Vitro
Fertilization (IVF) treatment. The clinic successfully extracted eggs and
sperm, created embryos, and implanted them. Mrs. Kapoor carried the
pregnancy to term and delivered a healthy baby boy. However, a routine
blood test six months later revealed a massive discrepancy. Extensive DNA
testing conclusively proved that while the child was genetically related
to Mr. Kapoor (the sperm), he had absolutely zero genetic relation to
Mrs. Kapoor. The clinic had catastrophically mixed up the petri dishes,
implanting an embryo created with a stranger's donor egg instead of Mrs.
Kapoor's extracted egg. The Kapoors sued the clinic under the Consumer
Protection Act for gross deficiency in service, demanding ₹10 Crores for
immense psychological trauma and the permanent deprivation of biological
motherhood.
cases.issues:
Is a fertility clinic providing IVF treatments classified as a "Service
Provider," subject to the Consumer Protection Act, 2019?

Does a catastrophic laboratory mix-up resulting in the implantation of
the wrong genetic material constitute an actionable "Deficiency in
Service"?

How does a consumer court quantify damages for profound psychological
trauma and the irreversible loss of genetic lineage?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. & Mrs. Kapoor)
The Kapoors argued they paid a premium for a highly specific medical
service: to have a child that was entirely genetically their own. By
failing basic laboratory identification protocols and implanting a
stranger's egg, the clinic committed a gross, inexcusable deficiency in
service. They argued the psychological devastation was infinite. Mrs.
Kapoor endured the physical toll of IVF and childbirth, only to discover
she was gestational, not a biological mother to her son. The trauma of
raising a child carrying a stranger's DNA, and the fear of the biological
mother eventually seeking custody, warranted maximum punitive and
compensatory damages.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Genesis IVF Clinic)
The Clinic admitted the human error but fiercely contested the ₹10 Crore
demand as extortionate. They argued that medical procedures carry
inherent risks of human error. They attempted to argue that the
fundamental objective of the service-giving the infertile couple a
healthy child-was technically achieved. They argued that Indian courts
typically award damages for tangible physical injury or financial loss,
not abstract emotional distress. They offered to refund the ₹15 Lakhs
procedure fee and pay a nominal penalty, arguing that a multi-crore
payout would bankrupt the clinic for a clerical error.
cases.judgment:
The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) ruled
overwhelmingly in favor of the Kapoors. The Clinic was found guilty of
severe deficiency in medical service and ordered to pay ₹2 Crores in
compensation for mental agony, alongside a full refund of the medical
fees. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Commission delivered a scathing indictment of the clinic's
negligence. The NCDRC affirmed that highly paid fertility treatments are
squarely within the ambit of "Service" under the Consumer Protection Act.
The judge ruled that an IVF clinic handles the very building blocks of
human life. The standard of care required is absolute precision. A petri
dish mix-up is not a mere "clerical error"; it is a catastrophic systemic
failure that permanently alters human lineage and destiny.

Addressing the quantum of damages, the Commission rejected the clinic's
argument minimizing emotional distress. The judge reasoned that the
injury suffered by Mrs. Kapoor was profound and irreversible-the
permanent theft of her biological motherhood. The psychological trauma of
the betrayal of trust and the lifelong implications for the child's
identity are immeasurable. While ₹10 Crores was deemed excessive, the
Commission awarded ₹2 Crores as both compensatory damages for severe
mental agony and punitive damages to enforce absolute laboratory
accountability in the booming, largely unregulated ART (Assisted
Reproductive Technology) sector.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a monumental precedent for Medical Negligence in Assisted
Reproductive Technology (ART). It establishes the principle that a
genetic mix-up during IVF constitutes a gross "Deficiency in Service"
under the Consumer Protection Act, and courts will award massive
compensation for the resulting pure psychological trauma and loss of
biological lineage, strictly elevating the standard of care for fertility
clinics.

cases.title: SEBI v. Rajiv Mathur
cases.facts:
Rajiv Mathur was a highly influential, billionaire industrialist. He
officially held no title, employment, or directorship in "Zenith Telecom
Ltd." However, his son was the CEO, and his brother-in-law was the CFO.
In reality, the board of Zenith Telecom never made a significant move
without secretly consulting Mathur, essentially acting in accordance with
his instructions.

In late 2024, Zenith Telecom entered highly confidential, disastrous
negotiations, realizing they were about to lose a massive 5G government
spectrum auction, which would crash their stock price. Mathur learned
this non-public information during a private dinner with his son. The
next morning, Mathur used his offshore portfolio managers to heavily
short-sell Zenith Telecom stock. When the news of the lost auction went
public a week later, the stock plummeted, and Mathur made a ₹50 Crore
profit. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) investigated
and charged Mathur with Insider Trading under the SEBI Act. Mathur argued
he was a total outsider, possessing no fiduciary duty to the company.
cases.issues:
Can an individual who holds no formal position or title within a company
be classified as a "Connected Person" or an "Insider" under SEBI
regulations?

Does the concept of a "Shadow Director" exist in Indian corporate law to
attach fiduciary liability to individuals who control the board from
behind the scenes?

Did trading on non-public information obtained through familial ties
constitute illegal Insider Trading?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (SEBI)
SEBI argued for a purposive interpretation of the Prohibition of Insider
Trading (PIT) Regulations. They asserted that Mathur was the classic
definition of a "Shadow Director"-a person in accordance with whose
directions or instructions the Board of Directors of a company is
accustomed to act (recognized under the Companies Act, 2013). Because he
functionally controlled the company, he was a "Connected Person" with a
fiduciary duty. Furthermore, SEBI argued that anyone who receives
Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) and trades on it,
regardless of their official title, commits the offense of insider
trading, as it destroys market parity and defrauds retail investors.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Rajiv Mathur)
Mathur argued a strict, literal defense. He possessed no contract, no
salary, and no legal authority within Zenith Telecom. He argued that
familial advice over dinner does not legally transform a private citizen
into a corporate fiduciary. He contended that Insider Trading laws are
meant to penalize rogue executives who breach their duty to their
shareholders. Since he had no duty to Zenith's shareholders, he was
merely a savvy trader acting on market rumors. Prosecuting outsiders for
acting on gossip severely overreaches SEBI's regulatory mandate.
cases.judgment:
The Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT) ruled in favor of SEBI. Rajiv
Mathur was found guilty of Insider Trading, ordered to disgorge the
entire ₹50 Crore illicit profit, and banned from the securities market
for five years. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Tribunal delivered a robust judgment closing the loopholes of
corporate subterfuge. The judge heavily relied on the broad definitions
within the SEBI (PIT) Regulations. The Court affirmed the existence of
the "Shadow Director" concept in Indian law. Evidence showed the Zenith
board functioned as a mere puppet for Mathur's directives, establishing
him as a "Connected Person" under the law.

More broadly, the Tribunal ruled that the modern offense of Insider
Trading relies on "Information Parity." The law strictly prohibits any
person who is in possession of Unpublished Price Sensitive Information
(UPSI) from trading on it. How Mathur acquired the information (whether
through a boardroom or a dinner table with the CEO) is legally
irrelevant. He possessed asymmetrical, confidential knowledge capable of
moving the market, and he weaponized it for massive personal gain.
Allowing shadow controllers or family members to exploit confidential
data would shatter the integrity of the financial markets.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case significantly broadens the scope of Insider Trading Liability
(SEBI PIT Regulations) and validates the concept of a Shadow Director. It
establishes the legal principle that anyone in possession of Unpublished
Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) who trades on it commits an offense,
regardless of whether they hold a formal fiduciary position or title
within the company, prioritizing absolute market parity.

cases.title: Sharma v. Apollo Diagnostics
cases.facts:
Mr. Sharma, experiencing chronic, severe headaches, visited Apollo
Diagnostics for a routine MRI scan. The radiologist misread the scan,
failing to identify a small, distinct 5-millimeter aneurysm (a weakened
blood vessel wall) in Sharma's brain, and issued a "clean bill of
health." Eight months later, the aneurysm ruptured. Sharma suffered a
massive hemorrhagic stroke, leaving him permanently paralyzed on his left
side.

Subsequent reviews of the original MRI by independent neurosurgeons
confirmed the aneurysm was clearly visible at the time of the first scan.
Sharma sued Apollo Diagnostics for medical negligence. During the trial,
medical experts testified that if the aneurysm had been detected early,
surgery would have provided a 40% chance of successfully preventing the
rupture. Apollo Diagnostics argued that since the chance of successful
surgery was less than 50%, the statistical probability was that he would
have suffered the stroke anyway, meaning their negligence was not the
proximate cause of his paralysis.
cases.issues:
Is a diagnostic center liable for medical negligence when a misdiagnosis
deprives a patient of a statistical chance of recovery, even if that
chance was less than 50%?

Does Indian tort law recognize the "Loss of Chance" doctrine as an
actionable injury?

How does the Court determine proximate causation when dealing with
probabilistic medical outcomes?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Mr. Sharma)
The Plaintiff argued for the adoption of the "Loss of Chance" doctrine.
He conceded that surgery was not a 100% guarantee, but he argued that
Apollo's gross negligence entirely stole his 40% chance of survival and a
healthy life. He argued that in modern medicine, a 40% chance is a
massive, tangible asset. By failing to diagnose the condition, the clinic
doomed him. He asserted that denying compensation simply because the odds
were slightly below 50% is a draconian mathematical technicality that
allows negligent diagnostic centers to escape liability for lethal
mistakes made on critically ill patients.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Apollo Diagnostics)
The Defendant relied strictly on traditional tort principles of causation
(the "But-For" test). They argued that the plaintiff must prove, on the
balance of probabilities (greater than 50%), that the negligence caused
the injury. Medical experts agreed there was a 60% chance the aneurysm
might have ruptured even with surgery or during the surgery itself.
Therefore, statisically, the underlying medical condition, not the
misdiagnosis, was the proximate cause of the paralysis. They argued that
compensating for a "lost chance" radically alters tort law, punishing
doctors for the progression of natural diseases.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of Mr. Sharma, formally recognizing the
"Loss of Chance" doctrine. Apollo Diagnostics was held liable and ordered
to pay proportional damages. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a highly progressive, modern interpretation of
medical torts. The judge acknowledged the traditional "all-or-nothing"
causation rule but ruled it fundamentally unjust in cases of delayed
medical diagnosis. When a patient goes to a diagnostic center, they are
paying specifically for early detection to secure every possible chance
of survival.

The Court ruled that the "injury" in this case was not the stroke itself,
but the deprivation of the 40% opportunity to avoid the stroke. A 40%
chance of life is a legally recognizable, valuable right. The
radiologist's blatant negligence directly destroyed that right. However,
applying equity, the Court did not award 100% of the damages for the
paralysis. Since the negligence deprived him of a 40% chance of recovery,
Apollo Diagnostics was ordered to pay exactly 40% of the total quantified
damages for his medical care and loss of livelihood. This perfectly
balances the accountability of the clinic with the statistical reality of
the patient's underlying disease.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case introduces the "Loss of Chance" Doctrine into Indian Medical
Torts. It establishes the legal principle that a patient can claim
damages for medical negligence even if their chance of recovery was less
than 50%, provided the misdiagnosis demonstrably destroyed a substantial,
quantifiable statistical opportunity to avoid harm, with damages awarded
proportionally to the lost chance.

cases.title: Reliance Infrastructure v. State of MP
cases.facts:
Reliance Infrastructure entered into a massive contract to purchase 500
acres of land from a consortium of farmers in Madhya Pradesh to build a
solar power plant. The contract was explicitly drafted as a "Contingent
Contract" under Section 31 of the Indian Contract Act. Clause 5 stated:
"This sale is strictly contingent upon the Buyer securing environmental
clearance from the State Pollution Control Board within 12 months. If
clearance is not obtained, the contract is void."

Eleven months into the contract, property prices in the region tripled
due to a new government highway project. The farmers, realizing they
could sell the land for much more, used immense local political influence
to maliciously block and delay Reliance's environmental clearance
application at the Pollution Board. Consequently, the 12-month deadline
passed without clearance. The farmers immediately declared the contract
void and attempted to sell to a third party. Reliance filed a suit for
Specific Performance, arguing the farmers sabotaged the contingency.
cases.issues:
Under Section 31 of the Indian Contract Act, does a contract become void
if the contingent event fails to happen due to the deliberate, malicious
sabotage by the party seeking to avoid the contract?

Does the equitable principle that "a man cannot take advantage of his own
wrong" override the strict literal deadline of a contingent contract?

Can a court grant Specific Performance of a contract where the technical
condition precedent was not met?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Reliance Infrastructure)
Reliance argued a classic equitable defense. They asserted that they had
completed all necessary paperwork and the clearance was imminent, but the
farmers deliberately weaponized their political connections to stall the
bureaucratic process until the deadline expired. Reliance relied on the
principle that a condition is deemed fulfilled if its non-fulfillment is
caused by the very party obligated by the contract. Allowing the farmers
to void the contract based on a failure they maliciously engineered would
be allowing them to profit from their own fraud.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Farmers Consortium)
The Farmers argued a strict, literal interpretation of the contract.
Clause 5 was absolute: no clearance within 12 months, no contract. They
argued that securing clearances was solely Reliance's responsibility. The
farmers contended they were merely exercising their legal right to walk
away from a voided contract and secure a better market price. They argued
that courts cannot rewrite commercial contracts or waive strict deadlines
simply because a bureaucratic process was slow, putting the burden of
proof entirely on Reliance to prove an almost impossible standard of
secret political sabotage.
cases.judgment:
The Commercial Court ruled in favor of Reliance Infrastructure. The Court
held the contingency was deemed fulfilled due to the defendants' bad
faith, and ordered the farmers to execute the sale deed (Specific
Performance). The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a severe blow to commercial bad faith. The judge
acknowledged the strict nature of contingent contracts under Section 31.
However, contract law is fundamentally governed by the overarching duty
of good faith. The Court analyzed the evidence (RTI requests,
communications) which clearly demonstrated that the farmers had actively
petitioned and pressured local officials to delay the specific file.

The judge invoked the fundamental equitable maxim: Nullus commodum capere
potest de injuria sua propria (No man can take advantage of his own
wrong). If a promisor prevents the happening of a condition precedent,
the condition is legally excused, and the promisor's obligation becomes
absolute. The farmers deliberately choked the bureaucratic process to
kill the deal and secure a higher price elsewhere. The Court ruled that
equity will step in to neutralize this fraud. Because the failure of the
contingency was orchestrated by the defendants, the Court treated the
condition as fulfilled and mandated the specific performance of the land
sale at the original agreed price.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case strictly limits the abuse of Contingent Contracts (Section 31,
Indian Contract Act). It establishes the absolute equitable principle
that if a party deliberately and maliciously prevents the fulfillment of
a contingent condition to escape their obligations, the law deems the
condition fulfilled. The offending party cannot profit from their own
sabotage, and the contract becomes specifically enforceable against them.

cases.title: LexImperia Pvt. Ltd. v. JurisMind AI
cases.facts:
Aryan, a computer science graduate, founded LexImperia Pvt. Ltd.,
developing a highly popular educational platform named "Mera Lawyer."
Over two years, Aryan and his team manually curated, structured, and
annotated a massive, proprietary database of 50,000 highly probable CLAT
multiple-choice questions, integrating detailed historical contexts of
Indian Constitutional Law (specifically Articles 1-50). The database was
behind a paywall.

In 2026, a rival tech company, JurisMind AI, launched an advanced
generative legal chatbot. Upon analyzing JurisMind's outputs, Aryan
discovered the chatbot replicated LexImperia's unique constitutional law
annotations and specific MCQ structures verbatim. JurisMind admitted to
using automated web-scrapers to ingest "Mera Lawyer's" entire database to
train their Large Language Model (LLM), but argued they did not "copy"
the database for sale; they merely used it for machine learning,
generating new, independent text. LexImperia sued for copyright
infringement.
cases.issues:
Does scraping a proprietary, structured database of educational materials
to train a Generative AI model constitute copyright infringement under
the Copyright Act, 1957?

Does the act of "Text and Data Mining" (TDM) by a commercial AI entity
fall under the "Fair Dealing" exception for research under Section
52(1)(a)?

Is a structured compilation of legal questions and constitutional notes
considered an "original literary work"?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (LexImperia Pvt. Ltd.)
LexImperia argued that their database qualifies as a protected "literary
work" (compilation) under Section 2(o) of the Copyright Act. While
constitutional facts are public domain, the specific selection,
arrangement, and annotation of the CLAT MCQs required immense human
skill, labor, and judgment (the "Sweat of the Brow" doctrine). LexImperia
asserted that the intermediate step of JurisMind copying the entire
database onto their servers to train the LLM constituted an unauthorized
reproduction. Because JurisMind is a commercial competitor, their use of
the data destroys LexImperia's market and fundamentally fails the Fair
Dealing test.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (JurisMind AI)
JurisMind argued the "Idea-Expression Dichotomy." They claimed their AI
does not reproduce LexImperia's database; it merely analyzes it to learn
the statistical probability of legal language. Learning from data, they
argued, is not copying an expression. They heavily relied on the "Fair
Dealing" exception for research, arguing that machine learning is a form
of technological research essential for Indian innovation. If AI
companies must license every piece of data they ingest, the entire AI
industry would collapse.
cases.judgment:
The High Court ruled in favor of LexImperia Pvt. Ltd. The Court granted a
permanent injunction against JurisMind AI, ordering them to purge the
infringing data from their models and pay compensatory damages. The
Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a landmark ruling on AI and copyright. The judge
affirmed that LexImperia's highly structured database of constitutional
MCQs was an original compilation protected by copyright. The Court ruled
that the act of scraping and temporarily storing the database on
JurisMind's servers to train the algorithm was a direct, unauthorized
reproduction. The judge strictly narrowed the "Fair Dealing" exception,
stating that commercial text and data mining (TDM) designed to create a
competing commercial product does not qualify as non-profit academic
"research." The Court held that technological advancement cannot be
subsidized by the uncompensated theft of a creator's intellectual labor.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case sets a major precedent for AI Training Data and Copyright
(Section 14 & 52, Copyright Act). It establishes the legal principle that
commercial scraping and ingestion of proprietary databases for machine
learning constitutes unauthorized reproduction, and commercial AI
training does not qualify for the Fair Dealing exception, protecting the
economic rights of digital compilers.

cases.title: Siya v. Global Hospitals Trust
cases.facts:
Siya was admitted to Global Hospitals Trust for a routine, localized
surgery on her right knee. She signed a standard consent form authorizing
the specific knee operation. Dr. Mehta, a highly respected visiting
surgeon (not a salaried employee of the hospital), performed the surgery.
While Siya was under anesthesia, Dr. Mehta unilaterally decided to make
an exploratory incision on her left knee as well, suspecting a future
ligament tear, though it posed no immediate danger. Siya awoke with
bilateral incisions and prolonged, unnecessary rehabilitation. She sued
Dr. Mehta and Global Hospitals Trust for medical battery and gross
negligence. The Hospital sought dismissal, arguing Dr. Mehta was an
independent contractor for whose clinical decisions they bore no
vicarious liability.
cases.issues:
Is a corporate hospital vicariously liable for the unauthorized surgical
actions of a "visiting consultant" who is not a direct employee?

Does performing an unconsented, non-emergency exploratory procedure
constitute the civil tort of medical battery?

Does the doctrine of "Ostensible Agency" apply to modern corporate
healthcare settings?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Siya)
Siya argued that the unauthorized incision on her healthy knee was a
gross violation of bodily autonomy and constituted medical battery, as
she only consented to surgery on her right knee. Against the hospital,
she invoked the doctrine of "Ostensible Agency." She argued that she
approached Global Hospitals for treatment, paid the hospital's billing
department, and relied on the hospital's reputation. The hospital held
Dr. Mehta out to the public as their authorized agent. Therefore, the
hospital owes a non-delegable duty of care to the patient and is
absolutely vicariously liable for the battery committed on their
premises.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Global Hospitals Trust)
The Hospital relied on the traditional "Contract OF Service" vs.
"Contract FOR Service" distinction. They argued Dr. Mehta was an
independent expert (Contract for Service). The hospital merely provided
the infrastructure and the operating theater. They argued they cannot
control a highly specialized surgeon's independent clinical decisions
mid-surgery. Therefore, under the strict rules of vicarious liability
(Respondeat Superior), the master-servant relationship did not exist, and
Siya's sole remedy lay against Dr. Mehta individually.
cases.judgment:
The Civil Court ruled in favor of Siya. Both Dr. Mehta and Global
Hospitals Trust were held jointly and severally liable to pay exemplary
damages for medical battery. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court radically modernized healthcare liability. The judge ruled that
the unconsented incision on the left knee was a blatant medical battery,
discarding any defense of "clinical good faith" since no emergency
existed. Crucially, the Court pierced the "independent contractor" shield
used by corporate hospitals. Applying the doctrine of "Ostensible
Agency," the judge ruled that modern patients seek out corporate
hospitals based on institutional branding, not individual doctors. When a
hospital bills a patient and provides holistic care, they implicitly
guarantee the safety of the patient against unauthorized physical
violations on their premises. The hospital holds a non-delegable duty of
care and cannot escape liability for gross torts committed in its
operating theaters by hiding behind complex internal employment
contracts.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case bridges the gap in Vicarious Liability and Ostensible Agency in
Corporate Healthcare. It establishes the legal principle that corporate
hospitals are jointly liable for medical battery and negligence committed
by "visiting consultants" on their premises, prioritizing the patient's
reliance on the institutional brand over internal employment
technicalities.

cases.title: Anshu v. Teamhorn Electronics Pvt. Ltd.
cases.facts:
Anshu, a major electronics distributor, entered into a binding contract
with Teamhorn Electronics Pvt. Ltd. on February 1, 2026. Teamhorn agreed
to supply 100,000 highly specialized microchips for Anshu's proprietary
consumer devices at a fixed price by May 1, 2026. In March 2026, a
sudden, unprecedented geopolitical embargo completely halted the export
of a rare-earth mineral essential for manufacturing these specific chips.
Teamhorn could theoretically source the mineral from a secondary black
market, but the cost would increase their manufacturing expense by 800%,
bankrupting the company. Teamhorn invoked the doctrine of frustration
under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act and terminated the agreement.
Anshu sued for breach of contract and massive damages for his halted
production lines.
cases.issues:
Does an extreme, unforeseeable 800% escalation in manufacturing costs due
to a geopolitical embargo legally "frustrate" a fixed-price commercial
contract under Section 56 of the Contract Act?

Is commercial impossibility (financial ruin) recognized as a valid ground
for frustration in India, or must the impossibility be strictly physical
or legal?

Did Teamhorn Electronics assume the inherent risk of supply chain
volatility when signing a fixed-price contract?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Anshu)
Anshu argued that Indian courts apply a highly restrictive interpretation
to Section 56. Relying on Energy Watchdog v. CERC, he argued that mere
commercial hardship, unprofitability, or astronomical cost escalations do
not equate to "impossibility." Teamhorn had not lost the physical
capacity to make the chips; it just became a terrible financial bargain
for them. Anshu argued that sophisticated corporate entities entering
into fixed-price contracts expressly assume the risk of raw material
price fluctuations. Allowing Teamhorn to abandon the contract would
destroy commercial certainty in the electronics sector.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Teamhorn Electronics)
Teamhorn argued that the embargo fundamentally altered the foundational
basis of the contract. They argued that an 800% increase is not a mere
"fluctuation" but a catastrophic, unforeseeable "black swan" event. They
contended that forcing a company into literal bankruptcy to fulfill a
contract is commercially absurd and constitutes practical
"impossibility." They argued that the fundamental purpose of the
agreement-a mutually beneficial commercial exchange-was completely
destroyed by the sudden absence of the vital rare-earth mineral in the
legitimate global market.
cases.judgment:
The Commercial Court ruled in favor of Anshu. The defense of frustration
was rejected, and Teamhorn Electronics was held liable for breach of
contract and ordered to pay compensatory damages. The Plaintiff
prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
The Court delivered a rigid enforcement of commercial contracts. The
judge reaffirmed that the threshold for Section 56 (Frustration) in India
is exceptionally high. The Court ruled that physical or legal
impossibility (e.g., the factory burning down, or the government outright
banning the final chip) triggers frustration. However, severe economic
hardship, even if it leads to corporate bankruptcy, does not. The Court
noted that Teamhorn could still physically source the materials, albeit
at a ruinous cost. The judge reasoned that fixed-price contracts exist
precisely to allocate the risk of market volatility. If parties wish to
be protected from extreme supply chain shocks, they must explicitly draft
detailed Force Majeure clauses covering price escalations. The judiciary
will not rewrite a bad bargain under the guise of frustration.
cases.legalPrinciples:
This case reinforces the strict interpretation of the Doctrine of
Frustration (Section 56, Indian Contract Act). It establishes the
absolute legal principle that extreme commercial hardship, astronomical
cost escalations, or supply chain disruptions do NOT constitute legal
impossibility, enforcing the sanctity of fixed-price commercial
contracts.

cases.title: Soumya v. Devendra
cases.facts:
Soumya, a highly successful software architect, and Devendra, a wealthy
entrepreneur, married in 2020. Recognizing their independent wealth, they
signed a comprehensive, notarized Pre-Nuptial Agreement before the
wedding. The contract explicitly stated that in the event of a divorce,
neither party would claim alimony or maintenance from the other under any
statute. In 2026, the marriage irretrievably broke down. Soumya's startup
had recently failed, leaving her entirely bankrupt and without income.
During the divorce proceedings, she filed an application for interim and
permanent maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and Section 24 of the
Hindu Marriage Act. Devendra presented the Pre-Nuptial Agreement to the
Family Court, demanding her claim be dismissed as barred by their
explicit, signed contract.
cases.issues:
Are Pre-Nuptial agreements waiving the statutory right to maintenance
legally valid and enforceable under Indian family law?

Does an agreement to forfeit the right to maintenance violate Section 23
of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 (agreements opposed to public policy)?

Can a civil contract override the statutory, welfare-oriented mandate of
Section 125 of the CrPC?
cases.arguments:
A. Arguments for the Plaintiff/Appellant (Soumya)
Soumya argued that the pre-nuptial agreement is void ab initio in India.
She relied on Section 23 of the Contract Act, which invalidates any
agreement that defeats the provisions of any law or is opposed to public
policy. She argued that Section 125 of the CrPC is a social justice
statute designed to prevent vagrancy and destitution. A citizen cannot
"contract out" of a fundamental statutory right designed for public
welfare. Because she was currently bankrupt and unable to maintain
herself, enforcing the pre-nup would leave her destitute, blatantly
violating the legislative intent of Indian family law.

B. Arguments for the Defendant/Respondent (Devendra)
Devendra argued for the sanctity of autonomous contracts between
consenting, educated adults. He pointed out that Soumya was a highly
sophisticated professional when she signed the agreement; there was no
coercion or fraud. He argued that modern marriages are partnerships of
equals, and the law should evolve to respect pre-nuptial financial
planning. He contended that forcing him to pay maintenance completely
destroys the financial certainty they mutually agreed upon, and
paternalistic laws treating women as perpetual dependents are obsolete in
the 21st century.
cases.judgment:
The Family Court ruled in favor of Soumya. The Pre-Nuptial agreement was
declared void regarding the waiver of maintenance, and Devendra was
ordered to pay statutory maintenance. The Plaintiff prevailed.
cases.reasoning:
